title: How ecosystems change and heal: storms, wolves, mangroves and the patchwork of a landscape

summary.text: A storm fells trees in a forest every few years. A fire burns a hillside. A volcano buries a whole island in ash. So why is the world not bare by now? You find out with dice and a paper forest of 36 patches. Storms hit your forest 60 times, and you count how much old forest is left. You roast a pot of soil to find out where new plants come from. You follow the wolves who were brought back to Yellowstone, and sort what scientists are sure of from what they still argue about. Then you see how people in Tamil Nadu helped a dying mangrove forest grow back, mostly by letting the sea back in.
summary.art: A paper grid of 36 squares with small numbers written in some squares, two dice beside it, and behind it a hillside that is part bare, part grass, part young trees and part tall old forest.

intro.hook: Somewhere near your home, a plant is growing where nobody planted them. It may be a peepal seedling on a wall, grass in a crack, or moss under a dripping pipe. How did they get there? And what would that spot look like in 50 years if nobody touched it?
intro.text: In the first activity, Nobody Planted Me, you hunt for these plants and work out how each one arrived. They are the first step of a change that goes on in every bare place on Earth. In this unit you follow that change from a crack in a wall to a whole forest, and then to the question of how a damaged place heals.
intro.art: A small peepal seedling growing from a crack in an old painted compound wall, with a child looking closely at the roots.

outcomes: By the end I can say what a disturbance is, and explain why plants and animals return to a cleared place in a certain order.
By the end I can tell primary succession from secondary succession, using my roasted soil results.
By the end I can explain, with my Patchwork Test numbers, why a landscape is a patchwork of ages and how its mix can stay steady.
By the end I can tell what is well shown and what is still argued about the wolves of Yellowstone.
By the end I can explain why restoring a place means finding what blocks its recovery, with the mangroves of Pichavaram as my example.
By the end I can say why rivers and wetlands need their flow of water back, and what a wetland does in a flood.
By the end I can explain why the right goal is the ecosystem that belongs to a place, which is not always a forest.

terms.meaning: An ecosystem is all the living beings of one place, together with the soil, water, air and sunlight they use.
terms.example: A pond with its fish, plants, mud, water and the sunlight falling on it is one ecosystem. So is a patch of forest.
terms.art: A village pond drawn as a cut-away, showing fish, water plants, mud at the bottom and sunlight coming in from above.

terms.meaning: A disturbance is an event that kills or removes many living beings from a place in a short time.
terms.example: A cyclone that fells trees is a disturbance. So is a fire, a flood, a landslide, or a bulldozer.
terms.art: A gap in a forest where three big trees have fallen in a storm, with sunlight reaching the ground.

terms.meaning: Succession is the slow change in which living beings live in a place, one group after another, after a disturbance.
terms.example: A paddy field left alone grows weeds in the first year, bushes after a few years, and young trees after that.
terms.art: Four small pictures in a row of the same field: bare, weedy, bushy and then wooded.

terms.meaning: Pioneer species are the first living beings to settle in a bare or cleared place.
terms.example: Lichens on bare rock, grasses on a landslide and the fast-growing Macaranga tree in a forest gap are all pioneers.
terms.art: A grey rock with flat patches of lichen and one small tuft of grass in a crack.

terms.meaning: Primary succession is succession that starts on ground with no soil and no life, such as new lava or bare rock.
terms.example: The island of Surtsey rose from the sea near Iceland in 1963. Everything living there had to arrive from somewhere else.
terms.art: A black lava shore with one small green plant growing near the tide line and a seabird overhead.

terms.meaning: Secondary succession is succession that starts where the soil is still there after a disturbance.
terms.example: After a forest fire, the soil still holds seeds, roots and fungi. So new plants appear within weeks.
terms.art: A burnt hillside with black stumps and bright green shoots coming up from the ground between them.

terms.meaning: A seed bank is all the living seeds that lie waiting in the soil of a place.
terms.example: A handful of soil from under a weedy patch can hold dozens of seeds that you cannot see.
terms.art: A cut-away of soil with many tiny seeds scattered in the top layer, and one of them sprouting.

terms.meaning: An old forest is a forest that has grown for a very long time without being cleared. Scientists also call it old-growth forest.
terms.example: The great hornbill nests in holes in very large old trees. A young forest has no such trees yet.
terms.art: A huge old tree with a nest hole high in the trunk and a great hornbill at the hole.

terms.meaning: A patch is one area of land that differs from the land around it, in its age or in who lives there.
terms.example: A gap where one giant tree fell is a small patch. A burnt hillside is a large one.
terms.art: A forest seen from above with one round gap of young bright-green growth among dark old trees.

terms.meaning: A patchwork, or mosaic, is a landscape made of many patches of different kinds and ages lying side by side.
terms.example: From a hilltop in the Western Ghats you can see tea, grassland, young forest and old forest in one view.
terms.art: A view from above of a hilly landscape divided into patches of different greens, a brown field and a blue lake.

terms.meaning: An apex predator is a predator at the top of a food web. No other animal hunts the adults for food.
terms.example: Tigers in Nagarhole and wolves in Yellowstone are apex predators.
terms.art: A grey wolf standing on a snowy ridge above a valley with a river.

terms.meaning: A trophic cascade is a chain of changes that passes down a food web, from predators to plant-eaters to plants.
terms.example: Where sea otters eat sea urchins, fewer urchins eat the kelp, and the kelp forest grows.
terms.art: Three boxes joined by arrows going down: a wolf, an elk and a willow bush.

terms.meaning: An ecosystem engineer is a living being who changes the shape of a place, and so changes who else can live there.
terms.example: A beaver builds a dam across a stream and makes a pond. Elephants push over trees and make clearings.
terms.art: A beaver beside a dam of sticks, with a still pond behind the dam and a narrow stream below it.

terms.meaning: Restoration is work done by people to help a damaged ecosystem recover.
terms.example: At Pichavaram in Tamil Nadu, people dug channels so that the tide could reach a dying mangrove forest again.
terms.art: People with spades digging a narrow channel across a bare mudflat towards a line of mangrove trees.

terms.meaning: Natural regeneration is a place growing back by itself, from the seeds and roots already there and the seeds that arrive.
terms.example: A field next to a forest is fenced off from cattle. In a few years young trees come up without anyone planting them.
terms.art: A fenced field beside a forest, full of young saplings of different heights, with a bird dropping a seed.

terms.meaning: A reference site is a healthy place of the same kind nearby. People study it to learn what a damaged place could become.
terms.example: Before restoring a rainforest fragment in the Anamalai hills, scientists list the trees of the protected forest next to it.
terms.art: Two patches side by side: a thin weedy patch and a thick tall forest, with a person making notes in the tall forest.

terms.meaning: A wetland is land that is covered with shallow water, or soaked with water, for all or part of the year.
terms.example: Pallikaranai marsh in Chennai, the mangroves of Pichavaram and a village tank edge full of reeds are all wetlands.
terms.art: A marsh with reeds, shallow water, a purple heron and tall city buildings far behind.

terms.meaning: A tipping point is the point where a small extra change makes an ecosystem switch to a very different state that then keeps itself going.
terms.example: A clear lake that gets more and more sewage can turn green and cloudy quite suddenly, and then stay that way.
terms.art: Two pictures of the same lake: one clear with plants on the bottom, one thick green, with an arrow between them.

explanations.concept: Disturbance: places get cleared all the time
explanations.definition: A disturbance is an event that kills or removes many living beings from a place in a short time.
explanations.description: Forests, grasslands, rivers and reefs are disturbed again and again. A big tree falls and takes the neighbours down. A cyclone flattens a mangrove. A river in flood scrapes its banks. A fire runs through dry grass. People add more: they cut, burn, plough, mine and build. Disturbances differ in three ways. They differ in size, from one fallen tree to a whole island. They differ in how often they come. And they differ in what they leave behind. A fire may leave the soil with its seeds and roots. A lava flow leaves nothing living at all. What is left behind decides how recovery starts, as your roasted soil shows in The Soil Remembers. A disturbance is not always harm. The gap left by a fallen tree is the only place where many seedlings get enough light to grow.
examples: In a rainforest in the Western Ghats, one giant tree falling can open a gap as wide as a house plot.
On 18 May 1980 the volcano Mount St Helens in the United States blew out sideways and flattened forest for many kilometres.
A village tank that dries out fully in a drought year is a disturbance for the fish and the water plants.
explanations.art: A tall forest with one large fallen trunk, a bright gap in the leaves above, and small seedlings in the light on the ground.

explanations.concept: Succession: who comes back, and why in that order
explanations.definition: Succession is the change in which living beings live in a place, one group after another, after a disturbance.
explanations.description: The first to settle are the pioneer species. They are good at arriving and good at living in the open. Their seeds or spores are small and many, and travel on wind, water or birds. They grow fast in full sun. But why do they not stay for ever? The reason is that they change the place. They shade the ground. Their dead leaves and roots add to the soil and hold water in it. Some, such as lupines and other plants of the bean family, house bacteria in their roots who take nitrogen from the air. Plants need nitrogen to build their bodies. Now the place suits other plants better than before. Many pioneers need full sun to sprout, so their own seedlings do poorly in the shade they made. Slower plants whose seedlings bear shade grow up under them and, in time, over them. Animals follow the plants they need. This order is a tendency, not a timetable. Which seeds happen to arrive first also matters, and two patches cleared on the same day can go different ways.
examples: On an abandoned field in South India, grasses and touch-me-not come first, then shrubs such as lantana and Calotropis, then trees.
In a gap in the Western Ghats rainforest, Macaranga trees shoot up in the sun. Slow, shade-bearing trees rise beneath them over many years.
On new ash at Mount St Helens, prairie lupines were the first plants. Their fallen leaves added nitrogen, and their stems trapped other seeds blown by the wind.
explanations.art: A strip of land shown at five ages from left to right: bare soil, grasses, shrubs, young sun-loving trees, and tall trees with seedlings in their shade.

explanations.concept: Starting with nothing, and starting with soil
explanations.definition: Primary succession starts on ground with no soil and no life. Secondary succession starts where the soil, with its seeds, roots and tiny beings, is still there.
explanations.description: Primary succession is slow, because soil has to be made first. On bare rock, lichens are often the first to settle. A lichen is a fungus and an alga, or a bacterium, living as one body. They make weak acids that slowly dissolve the rock's surface. Dust and dead lichen collect in cracks, and mosses root in that. On a new island, the sea and birds do much of the work. On Surtsey, the first plant with roots and leaves was a sea rocket, found on the shore in 1965. Her seed had floated there. Later, seabirds nested on the island, and their droppings fed the soil. Plants grew thickest where the gulls lived. Secondary succession is far quicker. The soil already holds a seed bank, living roots, fungi and bacteria. In The Soil Remembers you compare the two starts in two pots. One pot keeps its seed bank and one has had it killed by heat.
examples: Krakatau, a volcanic island in Indonesia, blew apart in August 1883. Nine months later a visitor found no plants, and only one tiny spider. By 1886 there were mosses, ferns and beach plants.
A burnt grass slope in the Nilgiris is green again within weeks of the first rain, because the grass roots lived.
A new concrete wall has no soil. Its first settlers are algae, mosses and lichens, where water drips.
explanations.art: Left: a bare grey rock with a few lichens. Right: a burnt slope already full of green shoots. A label under each says how old the patch is.

explanations.description: For a long time textbooks said that every place moves toward one final, stable community, called the climax, and then stops changing. Today most ecologists say something different. Late in succession, change does slow down, and old forests can look the same for centuries. But they are not finished. Trees die and gaps open. The climate shifts. New species arrive. So an old forest is better described as changing slowly than as complete.
examples: Pollen in lake mud shows that after the last ice age, each kind of tree spread north across North America at a different speed and by a different route.
A sacred grove in Kerala may look unchanged for 200 years, yet every big tree in it will fall and be replaced.
Lantana, brought to India from the Americas in the 1800s, now grows in many old forests that had no such shrub before.

perspectives.explanation: A plant community is like one giant living being. It is born, grows up through fixed stages and reaches an adult form, the climax, which the climate of the region decides.
Each species spreads and grows according to their own needs and their own luck in arriving. A community is whoever happens to be living together in a place. There is no fixed end.
Gleason was closer to the truth about how communities form. But Clements was right that living beings change a place for each other, and that late stages change slowly.

explanations.art: An old forest with one very large fallen trunk covered in moss and seedlings, and young trees of different heights around it.

explanations.concept: A landscape is a patchwork, and the mix can stay steady
explanations.definition: A landscape is a patchwork of patches at different ages since their last disturbance. If disturbances come at a steady rate, the share of young, middle and old patches stays about the same, while each single patch keeps changing.
explanations.description: Walk through a large old forest and you cross gaps of every age. Here is last year's treefall, bright and full of weeds. There is a thicket of thin poles twenty years old. Beyond are giants. Each patch is moving through succession, and sooner or later each is knocked back. Why does the whole not end up all young or all old? You find the reason in the Patchwork Test. Each round, storms clear a few patches, and the same number of older patches grow up a step. When what is cleared equals what grows back, the mix stops changing. The American ecologists Herbert Bormann and Gene Likens described this for a forest in 1979. The mix matters to the residents. Some need open sun, some need thickets and some need giant old trees. A patchwork gives each a place, and lets them move when their own patch changes.
examples: In your Patchwork Test, about 22 of 36 patches were old forest from round 3 onward, though different squares were old each time.
In Kaziranga in Assam, floods, grazing and the yearly burning of old grass keep a patchwork of short grass, tall grass, wetland and woodland. Rhinos, deer and birds use different parts.
Elephants push over trees and open clearings. The clearings fill with young plants that deer and gaur feed on.
explanations.art: A forest from above as a quilt of patches in four shades of green, each labelled with an age: 1 year, 10 years, 40 years, 300 years.

explanations.description: If patches are almost never cleared, the sun-loving pioneers have nowhere to live. If patches are cleared very often, nothing has time to grow old. So it seems that a middle amount of disturbance should keep the most kinds of living beings. Your Patchwork Test, played with no storms, 6 storms and 12 storms, lets you check this on paper. Real studies give a mixed answer.
examples: Part 2 of the Patchwork Test: doubling the storms cut the old patches from about 22 to about 13.
A lawn mown every week holds very few kinds of plant. An unmown corner of the same park holds many more.
Rocks on a seashore that waves roll over every few months carry more kinds of seaweed than rocks that never move.

perspectives.explanation: The number of species is highest where disturbance is neither rare nor frequent. With too little, a few strong competitors crowd out the rest. With too much, only fast settlers live.
When real places are measured, the hump in the middle shows up only rarely. The reasoning behind it has gaps too. The idea should be dropped.

perspectives.who: Douglas Sheil and David Burslem, replying in 2013
perspectives.explanation: The idea still explains real patterns, especially among forest trees. It must be tested with care, comparing the same kind of place under different amounts of disturbance.

explanations.art: Three small landscapes side by side: one all dark old forest, one a mixed patchwork, one nearly all bare and grassy.

explanations.concept: The wolves of Yellowstone: what happened
explanations.definition: Wolves were removed from Yellowstone National Park in the United States by 1926 and brought back in 1995 and 1996. Elk numbers then fell, and some plants that elk eat began to grow taller in some places.
explanations.description: Park rangers and hunters killed the last wolves of Yellowstone in 1926. People then thought predators were harmful. With no wolves, the elk, who are large deer, became many. They ate young willow, aspen and cottonwood trees down to stubs. Beavers need willow for food and for their dams, and beavers became rare. In January 1995, 14 wolves caught in Canada were brought to the park. Another 17 came in 1996. The wolves bred and spread. On the park's northern range, the winter count of elk fell from about 17,000 in 1995 to about 8,000 in 2004, and it has fallen further since. In some valleys young aspen and willow have since grown taller than an elk can reach. Beaver colonies on the northern range rose from 1 in 2001 to 9 in 2011. A chain of changes like this, from predator to plant-eater to plant, is called a trophic cascade. That much is agreed. How much of it the wolves caused is argued about, and the next card tells you why.
examples: By the end of 2023 there were 124 wolves in 11 packs in Yellowstone, all descended from the wolves brought in and from wolves who walked in later.
In India, where tigers are protected in a reserve, the number of deer and wild pigs they hunt is held down in the same way.
On the coast of North America, sea otters returning to a bay were followed by fewer sea urchins and more kelp.
explanations.art: A wide snowy valley with a river, a pack of wolves on a ridge, a herd of elk below and young willows along the river bank.

explanations.concept: The wolves of Yellowstone: what scientists argue about
explanations.description: A short film from 2014, How Wolves Change Rivers, says that the wolves changed where elk dared to feed, that the trees came back, and that the rivers themselves changed their shape. It has been watched many millions of times. It is a clear and moving story. Most scientists who work in Yellowstone say it claims too much. Three things make the true answer hard to find. First, wolves were not the only change. In the same years, people outside the park hunted many elk, the numbers of cougars and grizzly bears grew, and there were dry years. Second, there is only one Yellowstone. Nobody can run the same park again without wolves and compare. Third, the answer depends on where you measure and what you measure. Notice what kind of argument this is. Nobody is arguing about whether wolves belong in Yellowstone. They are arguing about how strongly one returned animal can repair a whole place.
examples: Two teams measured the same willows from 2001 to 2020. One measured height and found a weak effect. The other measured the volume of the leafy crown and found a strong one.
Bison in northern Yellowstone have become many more since the 1990s, and they eat young trees too.
In the activity The Wolf Chain you sort eight claims from this story into agreed, argued and claimed too much.

perspectives.who: William Ripple, Robert Beschta and colleagues, Oregon State University
perspectives.explanation: The return of wolves, with other predators, lowered the pressure of elk on young trees. Aspen and willow have recovered strongly in many places. It is a clear trophic cascade.

perspectives.who: Tom Hobbs, David Cooper and colleagues, Colorado State University, 2024
perspectives.explanation: In a 20-year experiment, willows grew tall only where they were both fenced from browsing and given a raised water level by a small dam. Wolves alone have not restored the streams. In the first ten years, human hunters lowered the elk more than wolves did.

perspectives.who: The film How Wolves Change Rivers, 2014
perspectives.explanation: Wolves made elk avoid risky valleys. Trees returned, banks held firm, and rivers ran straighter. Scientists on both sides above say this part goes beyond the evidence.

explanations.art: A willow bush beside a stream with two scientists: one holding a measuring pole against its height, the other measuring round its leafy top.

explanations.concept: Why putting one piece back does not always rewind a place
explanations.definition: An ecosystem can settle into more than one lasting state. Once it has switched, undoing the first cause may not switch it back.
explanations.description: Think about the streams of northern Yellowstone. When the wolves went, elk ate the willows. With no willows, the beavers left. With no beaver dams, the streams ran faster and cut down into their beds. As a stream cuts deeper, the water under the ground beside it sinks too. Willow roots then cannot reach water easily, even if no elk ever bites them. So the place now holds itself in a new state: deep stream, low water, short willows, no beavers. Bringing back the wolves removes the first cause, but the later causes are still there. Lakes show the same thing. A clear lake that receives too much sewage turns green with algae. The algae shade out the bottom plants, who used to hold the mud down and shelter the tiny animals that eat algae. Cutting the sewage back to the old amount is then not enough. The Dutch scientist Marten Scheffer and others have studied such switches since the 1990s. How common they are in nature is still being worked out.
examples: In the Yellowstone experiment, willows behind small man-made dams grew taller, because the dam raised the water under the ground.
Some shallow lakes in the Netherlands stayed green for years after the sewage was cut. They cleared only when people also took out many of the fish who stir up the mud.
A coral reef that loses its plant-eating fish can become covered in seaweed, and young corals then find no bare rock to settle on.
explanations.art: Two cut-away pictures of a stream: one shallow and wide with a beaver dam, tall willows and water just under the grass, and one cut deep with dry banks and short willows.

explanations.concept: Restoration: find what is blocking recovery
explanations.definition: Restoration is work done by people to help a damaged ecosystem recover. Its first question is what is stopping this place from growing back by itself.
explanations.description: Most damaged places are trying to recover all the time. Seeds arrive, roots resprout and animals wander in. So a restorer asks what is in the way. Sometimes cattle or fire keep killing the seedlings. Then a fence or a fire line is enough, and the land regrows by itself. This is called natural regeneration. A review of 133 studies of tropical forests, published in 2017, found that naturally regrown forests held more kinds of living beings, on average, than planted ones. Sometimes the seeds cannot arrive, because the nearest forest is far away. Then people must bring them. In the Anamalai hills of Tamil Nadu, Divya Mudappa, T. R. Shankar Raman and their team have restored rainforest fragments among tea estates since about 2001. They remove weeds such as lantana and plant many kinds of local trees raised from wild seed. And sometimes the block is in the ground or the water. At Pichavaram near Chidambaram, mangroves had died over about half the forest. Villagers and scientists found that sea water was standing still in sunken ground and turning far too salty. From 1996 they dug channels to let the tide flow in and out. Six years later, most of that damaged ground had young mangroves on it. A restored place is not the same as one that was never damaged. In the Anamalai study, the planted fragments were well ahead of the unplanted ones after 7 to 15 years, and still behind the old forest beside them.
examples: Pichavaram: about 375 hectares were damaged before the work. About 65 hectares were still damaged six years after it began.
Anamalai hills: replanted fragments stored about half as much carbon again as fragments left alone, yet less than the old forest nearby.
A hillside beside a healthy forest, closed to cattle for ten years, usually needs no planting at all.
explanations.art: Three small scenes: a fence keeping goats out of young saplings, people planting mixed seedlings among tea bushes, and a channel bringing sea water into a mudflat.

explanations.concept: Rivers and wetlands: give the water back its path
explanations.definition: A river or a wetland is made by moving water. To restore one, people restore how the water flows: where it goes, how fast, and when it rises and falls.
explanations.description: A river is more than a channel. It floods and shrinks with the seasons, carries sand and silt, and lets fish swim up and down it. A dam blocks all three. On the Elwha river in the United States, two old dams were taken down between 2011 and 2014. It was the largest dam removal in that country. Salmon, who are fish that swim up from the sea to breed, were seen above both dam sites by 2016. The first years were hard: the mud that poured out killed most small river animals downstream, and some kinds of salmon have still not recovered. A wetland is land soaked with shallow water. It works like a towel on a sloping board, as you find in Wetland on a Board. It soaks up a rush of water and lets it out slowly. Pallikaranai marsh in Chennai covered about 5,500 hectares in 1965. Roads, buildings and a rubbish dump have left about 600 to 700 hectares. Many scientists link Chennai's worst floods, as in December 2015, partly to the loss of marshes and lakes like this one. The marsh that remains was made a protected wetland of world importance in 2022.
examples: Pichavaram: the cure was to bring back the tide's flow in and out, twice a day.
A tank bund in Tamil Nadu repaired so that the tank fills in the monsoon brings back reeds, fish and water birds within a year or two.
On the Elwha, sand carried down the freed river rebuilt beaches at the river's mouth.
explanations.art: A marsh with reeds and water birds in the front, a raised road cutting across it, and blocks of flats standing on filled land behind.

explanations.concept: The ecosystem that belongs to the place is not always a forest
explanations.definition: The goal of restoration is the kind of ecosystem that the place's own climate, soil and history support. In many places that is grassland, scrub, desert or marsh, not forest.
explanations.description: Many people think healing land means planting trees. But large parts of India were never forest. The dry plains of the Deccan, parts of Rajasthan and Gujarat, and the high grasslands of the Western Ghats have been open country for many thousands of years. Blackbuck, wolves, great Indian bustards, larks and thousands of kinds of grass and herb live there and nowhere else. Old government maps mark much of this land as wasteland. A study by M. D. Madhusudan and Abi Vanak, published in 2023, found that nearly 70 in every 100 parts of India's dry open ecosystems lay on land marked as wasteland. Fewer than 5 in every 100 parts were protected. Planting trees there does not restore anything. It replaces one old ecosystem with a plantation, and the grassland beings lose their home. So a restorer first asks what this place was, and looks for a reference site. A reference site is a healthy place of the same kind nearby. The same care applies to mangroves. Seedlings planted on open mudflats where mangroves never grew mostly die.
examples: On the Nilgiri plateau, the natural cover is a patchwork of shola forest in the folds and grassland on the slopes. Wattle and eucalyptus planted on the grass have harmed it.
The great Indian bustard needs wide, open, dry grassland to feed and to nest. A plantation of trees takes that away.
In the Rann of Kutch, salt desert is the natural ecosystem, and wild asses live there.
explanations.art: A wide dry grassland with blackbuck and a lark in the sky, and at one edge a square block of planted trees in straight rows with a red question mark over it.

explanations.concept: Following the idea further: atoms, energy and deep time
explanations.definition: Succession can be followed down to atoms and energy, and back through the history of the Earth.
explanations.description: Atoms first. Bare rock has almost no nitrogen that a plant can use, though the air above it is mostly nitrogen. The first settlers that matter most are often those who house nitrogen-catching bacteria, such as lupines and alder trees. Lichens dissolve minerals out of rock, a few atoms at a time. A soil is rock, air and dead bodies that living beings have mixed. Now energy. A young patch grows fast and adds wood quickly. An old forest adds wood slowly but holds far more carbon in total, in its trunks and its soil. Seeds sense all this. Many pioneer seeds lie in the dark soil for years. They sprout when they sense the fuller light and the bigger swings of day and night temperature that a gap brings. Now time. After the last ice age, forests moved north over thousands of years, each tree species at their own speed. And 66 million years ago an asteroid struck the Earth and most forests died. In the rocks of North America laid down just after it, the pollen of trees almost vanishes and fern spores take over. Ferns were the pioneers then, as they are on fresh landslides today. Some scientists read all this as plain chemistry and chance. Seeds sense, wait and choose their moment, and that is part of how a place heals.
examples: Wild tobacco seeds in North America sprout when they sense chemicals from smoke, which tell them a fire has cleared the ground.
Near a retreating Himalayan glacier, the ground freed from ice first grows mosses and small herbs, and shrubs only decades later.
The layer of fern spores above the asteroid layer is called the fern spike.
explanations.art: A zoom-in series: a lichen on rock, then mineral grains and a root with small round lumps on it, then a layer of rock with fern shapes in it.

agreed.text: After a disturbance, living beings return in a rough order, and the early settlers change the place for the later ones.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have followed this year by year on Surtsey since 1963, on Mount St Helens since 1980, and on thousands of abandoned fields.

agreed.text: Recovery is much faster where the soil with its seeds and roots is still there.
agreed.evidence: Burnt and logged land greens within a season. New lava and bare rock take decades to grow more than lichens and scattered plants. Your roasted soil shows the same thing in a pot.

agreed.text: A large natural landscape is a patchwork of patches of different ages.
agreed.evidence: Aerial photographs, satellite pictures and the ages of trees counted from their rings all show it, in every kind of forest and grassland studied.

agreed.text: Wolves were brought back to Yellowstone in 1995 and 1996, and the number of elk on the northern range then fell by more than half.
agreed.evidence: Wolves and elk have been counted there every year. Hunters, bears, cougars and dry years also lowered the elk, as well as wolves.

agreed.text: Where the cause of damage is removed and seeds can arrive, most damaged ecosystems begin to recover by themselves.
agreed.evidence: A 2017 review of 133 studies of tropical forests, and the regrowth at Pichavaram after the tide was let back in from 1996.

agreed.text: A restored ecosystem is usually poorer than one that was never damaged, for decades at least.
agreed.evidence: In the 2017 review and in the Anamalai hills study of 2019, restored forests had fewer kinds of living beings, or less carbon, than old forest nearby.

challenging.claim: Nature is in balance. Left alone, every place returns to the way it was.
challenging.who: A very old and common belief, and the climax idea of Frederic Clements, 1916
challenging.for: Many places do return to something like their earlier state. A burnt grassland looks the same two years later.
challenging.against: Some places switch to a new state and stay there. Climates change, species arrive and species are lost. Pollen records show that the mix of trees in a region has kept changing for thousands of years.
challenging.context: This card is about the old idea that each place has one natural state that it always returns to.

challenging.claim: Bringing back the wolves healed Yellowstone, and even changed its rivers.
challenging.who: The film How Wolves Change Rivers, 2014, and many news stories
challenging.for: Elk fell by more than half. Aspen and willow have grown taller in a number of places. Beaver colonies increased.
challenging.against: Hunters, bears, cougars and drought also cut the elk. In a 20-year experiment, willows on most streams stayed short unless the water level was raised as well. Careful measurements have not shown rivers changing course.
challenging.context: This card is about how much the wolves brought back to Yellowstone National Park changed the plants and rivers there.

challenging.claim: The best way to heal land is to plant as many trees as possible.
challenging.who: Many tree-planting drives around the world
challenging.for: Where the nearest forest is far away, seeds cannot arrive, and planting local trees speeds recovery. The Anamalai rainforest work shows this.
challenging.against: Natural regrowth often does better and costs less. Trees planted on natural grasslands, marshes or mudflats destroy the ecosystem that was there. Rows of one kind of tree are a plantation, not a forest.
challenging.context: This card is about whether planting trees is always the right way to restore damaged land.

challenging.claim: A tiny, very dense planted forest can become like a natural forest in about 20 or 30 years.
challenging.who: Followers of the planting method of the Japanese botanist Akira Miyawaki
challenging.for: Saplings planted close together in rich soil grow tall quickly, and a bare city plot becomes green and shady within a few years.
challenging.against: Many ecologists in India say there is little long-term measurement, that the method costs a great deal, and that it is used in dry places where dense forest never grew. Tall trees are only one part of a forest.
challenging.context: This card is about small, dense city plantations called Miyawaki forests, and whether they are real forests.

challenging.claim: Animals from another country can stand in for animals that have died out here.
challenging.who: Supporters of India's Project Cheetah, begun in 2022
challenging.for: India's own cheetahs died out about 70 years ago. Eight African cheetahs were brought from Namibia to Kuno in Madhya Pradesh in September 2022 and twelve from South Africa in 2023. Cubs have been born there since.
challenging.against: Critics such as the tiger scientist Ullas Karanth say Kuno is too small, that many of the first animals died, and that India's grasslands should be protected first. African cheetahs are also a different subspecies from the Asian one.
challenging.context: This card is about bringing a missing kind of animal back to a place by using animals from somewhere else.

big_questions.q: In the Patchwork Test, every square changed, but the count of old squares stayed near 22. So what is 'the forest': the squares or the mix?
big_questions.hint: Could you point to the forest on your grid? Is it in any one square?

big_questions.q: When a mangrove grows back after people dig a channel, who healed the forest: the people, the tide or the mangroves?
big_questions.hint: What did each one do? Could any one of them have done it alone?

big_questions.q: A restored forest has the same trees as before, but all of them are young. Is it the same forest?
big_questions.hint: Think of what an old tree has that a young tree of the same kind has not.

big_questions.q: If a place has changed many times over 10,000 years, which of its past states should people restore it to?
big_questions.hint: Who should choose? The people living there now, scientists, or nobody?

big_questions.q: A fallen tree is a death for the tree and a beginning for a hundred seedlings. Is a disturbance bad, good or neither?
big_questions.hint: Does your answer depend on who you ask: the tree, the seedlings or the hornbill?

big_questions.q: People are a cause of disturbance and also the ones who restore. Are we outside the ecosystem, or one of its animals?
big_questions.hint: Beavers flood valleys and elephants push down trees. Is what people do different in kind, or only in size?

story.title: The Water That Stood Still
story.note: A made-up story about real work. The Pichavaram mangrove forest near Chidambaram in Tamil Nadu is real. By the 1980s mangroves had died over about half of it. From 1996, the M. S. Swaminathan Research Foundation, the Tamil Nadu Forest Department and people of the nearby villages, among them Irular families, dug tidal channels in the sunken, stagnant ground and planted seedlings. Villagers helped to find the cause. Six years later most of the damaged ground had young mangroves. Irular women of Pichavaram do catch prawns by feeling for them with their hands. Thenmozhi, her mother Valli, her brother Murugan, Kamala akka and everything they say and do are imagined.
text: The seedlings were dying again.

Thenmozhi could tell from the boat, before anyone stepped out. Three hundred small mangroves stood in rows across the grey flat, each one planted by hand in the cool month of Thai. In Thai they had been green. Now, in the heat of Chithirai, their leaves were the colour of old paper.
"That is the third time," said her brother Murugan, who was seven and counted everything.

Kamala akka did not answer. She was the scientist who had come from Chennai two years ago, with a notebook, a floppy hat and more patience than anyone in the village had expected. She climbed out, squatted by the nearest seedling and rubbed a leaf between her fingers. It crumbled.

Thenmozhi's amma, Valli, was already walking away along the creek with her basket tied at her waist. Seedlings did not feed a family. Prawns did. Thenmozhi followed her, because that was her work on days without school. She waded in beside her mother, bent down and felt along the soft mud with both hands, the way her amma's amma had done. The tide was going out. The water slid past her wrists, cool, pulling gently toward the sea.

Here, along the creek, mangroves grew thick. Nobody had planted these. Their roots stood out of the mud like the fingers of a hand pressed down. And between the roots, Thenmozhi saw as she bent, there were babies. Dozens of them, each with two leaves, each sitting in mud that the creek had wet that morning and would wet again by evening.
"Amma. Who planted these small ones?"
"Nobody. The seeds float. The water brings them and leaves them." Valli pulled up a prawn, dropped it in the basket and moved on.

By noon the basket was a quarter full and Thenmozhi was thirsty. She walked back across the flat toward the boat. The ground here was different. It crunched. A white crust lay over the mud and broke under her feet into sharp flakes. In the middle of the flat the ground dipped, and in the dip lay a wide sheet of water, ankle deep, flat and bright as a steel plate.
Murugan was standing at its edge. "I dare you to taste it."
"It is sea water. I know what sea water tastes like."
"Then taste it."
She dipped a finger and licked it. Her whole mouth pulled tight. She spat, and spat again. It was sea water the way pickle is a mango. Murugan laughed so hard that he sat down in the crust.
Thenmozhi did not laugh. She stood looking at the bright water. A dragonfly crossed it. Nothing else moved. No pull at her ankles. No ripple going anywhere.
"When did this water come?" she asked.
"It is always here," said Murugan. "Since the big tide at the new moon. It just gets smaller."

Smaller. She looked at the white rim around the pool, a hand wide, where the water had been last week. The water was leaving, then. Only not the way it left the creek. It was leaving upward, into the sun. And the salt was staying behind.
She thought of her amma's rasam on the stove, forgotten once, boiled down to a dark spoonful that nobody could eat.
She ran.

Kamala akka was still by the dead rows, writing. Thenmozhi arrived without breath and pointed back at the pool, then at the creek, and then found some words. "In the creek the water comes and goes. Two times every day. The babies there live. Here it comes one time in a month and then it stands. It stands and the sun cooks it. Akka, taste it."
Kamala akka walked to the pool and tasted it. She was polite and did not spit, but her eyes watered.
"We have been bringing plants," she said slowly.
"Don't bring plants," said Thenmozhi. "Bring the creek."

It was Valli who told the others, that evening, in fewer words than her daughter had used. The old men said the ground had sunk since the big trees were cut, in their fathers' time, when the cutting was done one whole block at a time. Sunk ground holds water. Nobody had thought of that as a reason before, because nobody had asked them.

They dug in the month of Aadi, forty people with spades, the women carrying the mud away in headloads. One long channel ran from the creek to the middle of the flat, and short ones branched off it to both sides. From the bund it looked like the bones of a fish. Murugan counted the side channels and got nineteen.

Then the tide came. Thenmozhi stood in the main channel and felt it arrive, a cool push against her shins, brown and quick, carrying leaves and bits of stick. It filled the dip. Six hours later she came back and stood there again, and felt it pulling the other way, taking the old bright water with it out to the sea.

They planted that year too, along the channels. Kamala akka said they should do both. But in the next Thai, when Thenmozhi walked the flat with a stick to count for Murugan, she found more seedlings than anyone had put there. They stood in no rows at all. They grew wherever the tide had set them down.
She counted the ones in rows and the ones not in rows, and the ones not in rows won.
"Who planted those?" asked Murugan.
"Nobody," said Thenmozhi. "We only opened the door."
story.epiphany: For the parent: the story turns when Thenmozhi stops asking why the seedlings die and asks what the water is doing. The mangroves were never short of seeds. The standing water had become too salty for them. Once the tide could flow in and out, the forest began to plant itself. Restoration is often the removal of whatever blocks a place from recovering.
ask: Why did the mangrove seedlings die on the flat, when wild ones lived beside the creek?
The standing water was much saltier than the sea. Where did the extra salt come from?
What is the difference between bringing plants to a place and bringing back what the plants need?
The old men knew the ground had sunk. Why had nobody used what they knew before?
Think of a damaged place you know. What might be blocking that place from growing back?

games.title: Climb to Old Forest
games.context: This is a card and dice game about succession. Each player owns one bare patch of land. Living beings move in, in the order a real patch fills up, and storms knock the patch back. The first patch to become old forest wins.

printables.title: 24 settler cards to cut out (the stage is on the back)

items.f: Lichen. I grow on bare rock. I need only light, air and rain.
items.b: Pioneer. Lichens can live where there is no soil at all.

items.f: Moss. My spores blow on the wind. I need a damp bare surface.
items.b: Pioneer. Mosses settle in cracks and hold the first dust.

items.f: Grass. My seeds are light and many. I need full sun.
items.b: Pioneer. Grasses cover open ground within one season.

items.f: Touch-me-not. I creep over open ground. My roots house nitrogen-catching bacteria.
items.b: Pioneer. She grows in the open and adds nitrogen to poor soil.

items.f: Calotropis (erukku). My seeds fly on silk hairs. I like hot, open, poor ground.
items.b: Pioneer. Wind-carried seeds and a liking for open sun.

items.f: Macaranga tree. I grow very fast in a sunny gap. My seedlings die in shade.
items.b: Pioneer. A fast tree of sunny gaps, who cannot grow in shade.

items.f: Grasshopper. I eat grass in the open sun.
items.b: Pioneer. Grasshoppers follow the grass as soon as it grows.

items.f: Ants. We nest in open ground and carry seeds about.
items.b: Pioneer. Ants arrive early and move seeds into the soil.

items.f: Lantana bush. Birds drop my seeds. I need some soil and plenty of light.
items.b: Middle. Shrubs come once there is soil and before tall trees shade them.

items.f: Red-vented bulbul. I eat berries in bushes and drop the seeds elsewhere.
items.b: Middle. Bulbuls need shrubs with fruit, and they bring in new seeds.

items.f: Bamboo. I spread in thick clumps once there is soil that holds water.
items.b: Middle. Bamboo often fills land a few years after it was cleared.

items.f: Young neem tree. I grow up through the bushes toward the light.
items.b: Middle. Young trees rise where shrubs have sheltered the soil.

items.f: Butterflies. We need flowering bushes for nectar and leaves for our caterpillars.
items.b: Middle. Butterflies are most common where shrubs and flowers are many.

items.f: Tailorbird. I stitch my nest inside a big leaf in thick bushes.
items.b: Middle. She needs leafy shrubs or young trees to nest in.

items.f: Garden lizard. I bask on bushes and hunt insects there.
items.b: Middle. He needs bushes for basking and for cover.

items.f: Young fig tree. A bird left my seed here. I can start life in a crack or on another plant.
items.b: Middle. Fig trees arrive with birds once perches exist.

items.f: Great hornbill. I nest in a hole in a huge old tree.
items.b: Old forest. Only very old trees are big enough for her nest hole.

items.f: Lion-tailed macaque. I live high in the joined-up tops of tall trees.
items.b: Old forest. They need a tall, closed canopy to move and feed in.

items.f: Malabar giant squirrel. I leap from treetop to treetop and seldom come down.
items.b: Old forest. He needs tall trees whose crowns touch.

items.f: Orchid. I grow on the mossy branches of old trees.
items.b: Old forest. Such orchids need old, damp, mossy branches.

items.f: Slow shade tree. My seedling waits for years in deep shade.
items.b: Old forest. Their seedlings need the shade and damp soil of a grown forest.

items.f: Bracket fungus. I feed on big dead trunks.
items.b: Old forest. Big dead trunks exist only where big trees have lived and died.

items.f: Tree frog. I need damp air and wet tree holes all year.
items.b: Old forest. A tall closed forest keeps the air under it damp.

items.f: Giant old fig. I fruit when little else does, and feed a hundred animals.
items.b: Old forest. A fig tree needs many decades to grow this large.

printables.title: A patch track for each player: four boxes in a column, marked from the bottom Bare ground, Pioneers, Middle, Old forest

rules: Each player draws a patch track: four boxes in a column. From the bottom they are Bare ground, Pioneers, Middle and Old forest.
Shuffle the 24 settler cards. Put them in one pile with the story side up and the stage side hidden.
On your turn, roll the die. If you roll a 1, a storm hits your patch. Take the cards out of your highest filled box and put them under the pile.
If you roll 2 to 6, take the top card and read it aloud. Say which stage you think this being belongs to. Then turn the card to check.
You may keep the card only if your patch is ready. Pioneers can always move in. A Middle card needs 2 Pioneer cards on your track. An Old forest card needs 2 Middle cards.
Each box holds 2 cards. A card you cannot keep goes under the pile.
The first player with 2 cards in the Old forest box wins. Playing alone, count your turns and try to beat your own number.

setup.caption: 1. Draw a patch track of four boxes for each player.

setup.art: A pile of small cut-out cards on a table with a die beside it, and one card being read aloud by a child.
setup.caption: 2. Roll the die. On 2 to 6, read the top card and say which stage they belong to.

setup.art: A patch track with two cards in the Pioneers box and one in the Middle box, and a hand removing the Middle card after a roll of 1.
setup.caption: 3. Fill each box with 2 cards, from the bottom up. A roll of 1 is a storm.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 24 settler cards. 2. Each player draws a patch track of four boxes. 3. Shuffle the cards and pile them story side up.
flow.say: Each of us owns a bare patch of land. Living beings will move in, but only when the patch is ready for them.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Draw four boxes in a column. Label them from the bottom.
flow.parent: If you cannot print, copy the cards by hand on slips of paper. Write the stage on the back.
flow.context: This is the first step of Climb to Old Forest. Here you make the cards and the patch tracks.

flow.do: 1. Play two turns each as practice. 2. For each card ask where this being belongs, and why. 3. Turn the card to check.
flow.say: Read the card. What does this being need? Is that already on your patch? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Read your card. What do they need? Is your patch ready? Say why. Then check the back.

ask.q: Why can a hornbill not move into a patch of grass?
good: She nests in a hole in a huge old tree.
Grass has no big trees yet.
The trees she needs take a very long time to grow.

flow.parent: The point is the reason on the card. A player who guesses the stage wrongly still keeps the card if the patch is ready.
flow.context: This is the practice round of Climb to Old Forest. Here you learn when a being can move in.

flow.do: 1. Play in turn until someone has 2 cards in the Old forest box. 2. When a storm hits, ask what was lost and what is still there.
flow.say: A storm just hit your patch. What did you lose? What do you still have? How long will it take to get back?
flow.kid: Play until someone fills the Old forest box. When a storm hits, say what you lost.

check.q: A storm removes the Middle cards from a patch. The Pioneer cards stay. What kind of start is this?
options: Secondary succession, with soil still there
The end of the forest for ever
check.why: The lower stage is still there, as soil and seeds are after a real storm. So the patch regrows from part-way up. Choosing 'primary' means thinking every disturbance clears a place to bare rock, which is rare.

flow.parent: A game takes about 15 to 25 turns each. Old forest cards met early go back under the pile, which is how it is for a real hornbill who finds only bushes.
flow.context: This is the main part of Climb to Old Forest. Here you play until one patch becomes old forest.

flow.do: 1. Lay the winner's six cards in order from the bottom. 2. Ask what each stage gave to the next one.
flow.say: Look at the six cards in order. What did the pioneers make that the middle ones needed? What did the middle ones make?
flow.kid: Lay the winning cards in order. Say what each stage gave the next.

ask.q: What does each stage give the next?
good: Pioneers make soil and shade.
Shrubs give perches, so birds bring tree seeds.
Old trees give holes, big dead wood and damp air.

flow.context: This is the last step of Climb to Old Forest. Here you look at what the game showed.

games.title: Help or Harm?
games.context: This is a card game about restoring damaged places. Each card describes a real kind of place and a plan for it. You decide whether the plan helps, harms, or depends on something more. The back says what happened in real cases.

printables.title: 12 plan cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: A dry grassland where blackbuck and larks live. The plan: plant trees all over.
items.b: Harms. The grassland is the natural ecosystem here. Trees take the home of the grassland beings.

items.f: A mangrove patch is dying. Sea water stands still on sunken ground. The plan: dig channels so the tide flows in and out.
items.b: Helps. This was done at Pichavaram from 1996. Most of the damaged ground grew mangroves again.

items.f: An open mudflat where mangroves have never grown. The plan: plant ten thousand mangrove seedlings.
items.b: Harms, or fails. Mangroves were absent for a reason, such as waves or deep water. Most such seedlings die, and mudflat birds lose feeding ground.

items.f: A rainforest fragment among tea estates, full of lantana, far from other forest. The plan: clear the weeds and plant many kinds of local trees.
items.b: Helps. Seeds cannot arrive from far away. In the Anamalai hills, fragments restored this way recovered faster than those left alone.

items.f: A field beside a healthy forest. Cattle graze it bare. The plan: fence it and wait.
items.b: Helps. Seeds arrive from the forest next door. Natural regrowth often does as well as planting, or better.

items.f: An old dam, no longer used, blocks a river. Fish cannot swim up to breed. The plan: take the dam down.
items.b: Helps in the long run. On the Elwha river, salmon passed the old dam sites within two years. The first rush of mud killed many river animals.

items.f: A marsh at the edge of a city. The plan: fill part of it with soil and build flats.
items.b: Harms. A marsh soaks up flood water. Pallikaranai marsh in Chennai has lost most of its area, and the streets around it flood.

items.f: A park lost its wolves long ago. Deer have eaten the young trees down. The plan: bring wolves back.
items.b: It depends. In Yellowstone the deer became fewer and some trees grew back. Streams that had cut deep did not recover with wolves alone.

items.f: A lake is covered in water hyacinth. Sewage flows into it. The plan: pull out all the hyacinth once.
items.b: Not enough. Sewage feeds the hyacinth, so the plants grow back. The sewage must be stopped as well.

items.f: A cleared hillside. The plan: plant one kind of fast tree in straight rows.
items.b: Harms more than it helps. This is a plantation. It holds far fewer kinds of living beings than a forest of many trees.

items.f: A landslide scar in the middle of a healthy forest. The plan: leave it alone.
items.b: Helps. Seeds rain in from every side. Ferns, grasses and pioneer trees cover such a scar within a few years.

items.f: A regrowing field has no tall plants. The plan: put up tall poles as perches and plant a few fig trees.
items.b: Helps. Fruit-eating birds stop at perches and fig trees, and drop the seeds of forest trees there.

rules: Shuffle the 12 plan cards and pile them with the plan side up.
One player reads the top card aloud. On the count of three, everyone shows a thumb: up for helps, down for harms, sideways for it depends.
Each player gives one reason before the card is turned.
Turn the card and read the back. A player whose thumb matches the back wins a bean. 'Not enough' counts as sideways.
A player who gave the reason on the back wins a second bean.
When the pile is finished, the player with the most beans wins. Playing alone, count how many of the 12 you got right.
