setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 12 plan cards. Pile them plan side up.

setup.art: Three children holding out a thumb each: one up, one down, one sideways, while a fourth reads a card.
setup.caption: 2. Read a plan. Show thumb up, down or sideways. Give your reason.

setup.art: A card turned over to show its back, and a child taking a bean from the bowl.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card. A matching thumb wins a bean.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 12 plan cards and shuffle them. 2. Put a bowl of beans in the middle. 3. Explain the three thumbs.
flow.say: Each card is a damaged place and a plan to fix it. Some plans help. Some do harm. Some need something more.
flow.kid: Shuffle the cards. Thumb up means helps. Thumb down means harms. Sideways means it depends.
flow.context: This is the first step of Help or Harm? Here you get the cards and beans ready.

flow.do: 1. Read the top card aloud. 2. Count to three. 3. Everyone shows a thumb and gives a reason. 4. Turn the card and read the back.
flow.say: Before you choose, ask two things. What was this place before? What is stopping it from growing back?
flow.kid: Read the plan. What was this place before? What blocks it now? Show your thumb and say why.

ask.q: What two questions help you judge any plan?
good: What kind of ecosystem belongs here?
What is blocking it from recovering?

flow.parent: Disagreeing with the back is fine if the reason is good. Several of these are argued about among scientists too.
flow.context: This is the main part of Help or Harm? Here you judge each plan and give a reason.

flow.do: 1. Sort the cards into helps, harms and depends. 2. Ask what the helpful plans have in common.
flow.say: Look at the plans that helped. What do they have in common? What do the harmful ones have in common? Why?
flow.kid: Sort the cards into three heaps. What do the helpful plans share? Say why.

check.q: What do most of the helpful plans do?
options: Add as many plants as possible
Bring in new kinds from far away
check.why: The helpful plans take away a block: cattle, a dam, standing salt water, or the distance seeds must travel. Choosing 'add as many plants as possible' fits the plans that failed on the grassland and the mudflat.

flow.context: This is the last step of Help or Harm? Here you look for what the helpful plans share.

experiments.title: The Patchwork Test: after 60 storms, how much old forest is left?
experiments.context: In this experiment a paper grid of 36 squares is a forest, and each square is one patch. Every round is ten years. In each round, dice send 6 storms that clear 6 patches. A cleared patch needs three rounds to become old forest again. You count the patches of each age after every round.
experiments.question: Storms clear 6 of the 36 patches every ten years. After 100 years and 60 storms, how many patches are old forest? Does that number keep falling?
experiments.predict: Guess first. After 10 rounds and 60 storms, how many of the 36 patches will be old forest: none, about 10, about 20, or all 36? Will the number go on falling round after round? Say why you think so, and write it down.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same rules in every round: the same number of storms, and three rounds for a patch to grow old. Count every square in every round, and check that the four counts add up to 36. In part 2, change only the number of storms.

materials.item: a sheet of plain A4 paper
a ruler and a pencil
dice, of two colours if you have them (one die rolled twice also works)
a notebook for the table
graph paper or a squared maths notebook page

schedule.what: Draw the forest. Send 6 storms a round for 10 rounds, counting each time, and draw the graph. Then try 12 storms a round and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for every round of both parts. Draw the old forest counts of both parts on one line graph, in two colours. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: 6 storms in every round
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished table can look like. Your numbers will differ, because dice are chance.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a grid of 6 by 6 empty squares, the columns numbered 1 to 6 along the top and the rows numbered 1 to 6 down the side.
setup.caption: 1. Draw 36 squares. Number the columns and rows 1 to 6. An empty square is old forest.

setup.art: A child rolling two dice of different colours and writing the number 1 in the square where that column and row meet.
setup.caption: 2. Roll two dice for each storm. Write the round's number in the square that is hit.

setup.art: The grid after four rounds with the numbers 1, 2, 3 and 4 scattered in some squares, some crossed out and rewritten, and a notebook table beside it.
setup.caption: 3. After each round, count the squares by their number: this round, last round, the round before, and older or blank.

flow.do: 1. Draw a square 18 centimetres wide. 2. Divide it into 6 columns and 6 rows, each 3 centimetres wide. 3. Number the columns 1 to 6 along the top and the rows 1 to 6 down the side. 4. In the notebook draw a table with the five columns listed above.
flow.say: This grid is a forest of 36 patches. Every patch is old forest today, so every square is empty. Let's draw the table.
flow.kid: Draw 6 columns and 6 rows. Number them 1 to 6. Every empty square is old forest. Draw the table.
flow.parent: If you have one die, roll it twice: the first roll is the column and the second is the row. Decide this before you start and keep to it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Patchwork Test. Here you draw a forest of 36 patches and a table for your counts.

flow.do: 1. Explain the rules: 6 storms each round, and a cleared patch needs three rounds to grow old again. 2. Ask for the guess and the reason. 3. Write both down.
flow.say: Ten rounds will bring 60 storms, and there are only 36 patches. How much old forest will be left? Will it keep shrinking? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how many old patches after 10 rounds. Will the number keep falling? Say why. Write it down.

good: 60 is more than 36, so none will be left.
Patches grow back, so some will always be old.
It will fall at first and then stop.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children, and many adults, say that nothing will be left, because 60 storms are more than 36 patches.
flow.context: This step of the Patchwork Test is for guessing. You guess before you roll any dice.

flow.do: 1. Round 1: roll the two dice 6 times. Each time, write 1 in the square that is hit. 2. If a square is hit twice in a round, do nothing the second time. 3. Count the squares for the table. 4. Round 2: roll 6 times and write 2. Cross out an older number if a square is hit again. 5. Count again. Then play round 3.
flow.say: A square with this round's number is bare. Last round's number means grass. The number before that means young trees. Older numbers and empty squares are old forest.
flow.kid: Roll 6 storms. Write the round number in each square hit. Then count the four kinds. Play 3 rounds.
flow.parent: In round 3, for example, a 3 is bare, a 2 is grass, a 1 is young trees and an empty square is old forest. The four counts must add up to 36.
flow.context: This is the first playing step of the Patchwork Test. Here you play three rounds and learn how to count the patches.

flow.do: 1. Play rounds 4 to 10 in the same way. 2. After each round, fill in one row of the table. 3. Check that the row adds up to 36. 4. After round 6, stop and ask what the child notices about the old forest column.
flow.say: Look down the old forest column so far. What do you notice? What do you think the next four rounds will do? Why?
flow.kid: Play rounds 4 to 10. Count after each one. What is the old forest column doing?

ask.q: What do you notice in the old forest column?
good: It fell for three rounds and then stopped falling.
It goes up and down by one or two, around 21 or 22.
Different squares are old each time, but the count is nearly the same.

flow.parent: One of you rolls and one writes. From round 4 on, a square showing a number three or more rounds old counts as old forest. A computer ran these rules 4,000 times: old forest settled at 19 to 24 patches in almost every run.
flow.context: This is the long step of the Patchwork Test. Here you play rounds 4 to 10 and count after each one.

flow.do: 1. Draw a line graph of the old forest count for rounds 0 to 10. Round 0 is 36. 2. Ask for the claim, the evidence and the reason, in that order. 3. Only then give the explanation below.
flow.say: What do you think is true about this forest? Which numbers show it? Why does the line go flat? After you answer, I will tell you how scientists explain it.
flow.kid: Draw the old forest line. What is true about this forest? Which numbers show it? Why does the line go flat?

ask.q: Why does the old forest count stop falling?
good: Each round, about as many patches grow old as are cleared.
Storms clear 3 or 4 old patches a round, and 3 or 4 young patches become old.
The patches keep changing but the gains and losses match.

flow.parent: After your child has answered, explain: storms clear 5 or 6 patches a round, and 3 or 4 of them are old. In each round, 3 or 4 patches of young trees escape the storms and become old. When what is lost equals what is gained, the count stays level. Scientists call this a steady state.
flow.context: This step of the Patchwork Test turns your table into a graph and asks you to explain it.

flow.do: 1. Draw a fresh grid of 36 empty squares. 2. Ask for a new guess and a reason. 3. Play 5 rounds with 12 storms in each round. 4. Count after each round and fill in a second table.
flow.say: Now there are 12 storms a round. People have added their fires and cutting to the storms. Will the old forest go to zero this time? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw a new grid. Now roll 12 storms each round. Guess first, and say why. Play 5 rounds.
flow.parent: With 12 storms the old forest settles at 10 to 16 patches, usually about 13, and bare ground at about 10. It still levels off, at a lower number.
flow.context: This is part 2 of the Patchwork Test. Here you double the storms and see what changes.

flow.do: 1. Put the two tables side by side. 2. Add a third forest in your head: no storms at all, so 36 old patches. 3. Use this made-up rule: grasshoppers need at least 3 grass patches, and a hornbill family needs at least 15 old patches. 4. Ask who can live in each forest.
flow.say: Here are three forests. Who can live in the forest with no storms? With 6? With 12? Which forest has room for both? Why?
flow.kid: Compare your two tables. Grasshoppers need 3 grass patches. Hornbills need 15 old patches. Who can live in each forest?

check.q: A forest is hit by storms at the same rate for hundreds of years. What happens to its mix of young and old patches?
options: It swings from all young to all old
check.why: When patches are cleared and regrow at steady rates, the gains and losses match, so the mix stays about the same. Choosing 'all bare' counts the storms but forgets the regrowth. Choosing 'all old' forgets the storms.

flow.parent: The rule for grasshoppers and hornbills is made up for this test. Real animals do need a least amount of the right kind of patch, but the numbers differ for each.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Patchwork Test. Here you compare three forests: no storms, 6 storms and 12 storms.

experiments.title: The Soil Remembers: where do the first plants come from?
experiments.context: In this three-week experiment you take soil from a weedy place and split it into two pots. A grown-up roasts the soil for one pot, which kills the seeds in it. You water both pots and plant nothing. You find out whether new plants come from the soil or from outside.
experiments.question: If you plant nothing, will plants come up in a pot of soil? And will they still come up if the soil has been roasted first?
experiments.predict: Guess first. On day 21, how many plants will each pot have? If any plants grow in the roasted pot, where could their seeds have come from? Say why you think so, and write it down.
experiments.fair_test: Mix all the soil well before you split it, so that both pots start with the same soil. Use pots of the same size. Give both the same water and the same windowsill. The only difference is the roasting.
results_table: Anything else I see (moss, green film, fungus, ants)

materials.item: soil from a place where weeds grow, such as an old plant pot, the foot of a street tree or a garden edge
paper cups or small pots of the same size
an old kadai or tawa and a steel spoon, for roasting soil
a plate to stand the pots on
a tablespoon, a marker pen and a newspaper
a bright windowsill or balcony ledge

experiments.safety: A grown-up roasts the soil and pokes the holes in the cups. Hot soil smells strongly, so open a window. Let it cool fully before a child touches it. Wash your hands after touching soil.

schedule.what: Collect and mix the soil. Roast half of it. Fill the two pots, water them and write your guess.
Look closely at both pots. Count any seedlings.
Count the seedlings in each pot. Note anything else you see.
Count again. Are there different kinds of plant?
Count for the last time, compare the pots and explain.

experiments.record: Fill in the table on days 4, 7, 14 and 21. On day 21 draw both pots from above. Then write what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

setup.art: A heap of dark soil on a newspaper being mixed with a spoon, with two empty paper cups beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Mix the soil well. Divide it into two equal heaps.

setup.art: An adult stirring soil in an old kadai on a gas stove, with a window open behind.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up roasts one heap for 15 minutes, then lets it cool.

setup.art: Two paper cups of soil on a plate on a windowsill, labelled 'plain' and 'roasted', being watered with a tablespoon.
setup.caption: 3. Fill one pot with plain soil and one with roasted soil. Water both. Plant nothing.

setup.art: The same two cups three weeks later: the plain one full of small mixed seedlings, the roasted one bare except for one tiny plant.
setup.caption: 4. Count the plants in each pot on days 4, 7, 14 and 21.

flow.do: 1. Collect about 4 tumblers of soil from a place where weeds grow. 2. Tip it on a newspaper and pick out stones and plants. 3. Mix it well with a spoon. 4. Divide it into two equal heaps.
flow.say: We will plant nothing in this soil. Do you think anything will grow? Where would it come from? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Mix the soil well. Make two equal heaps. Will anything grow if you plant nothing? Say why.
flow.parent: Shop-bought potting mix often has few seeds. Soil from under weeds, from an old pot or from a roadside tree base works best. Take the top three or four centimetres, where most seeds lie.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Soil Remembers. Here you collect soil, mix it and split it in two.

flow.do: 1. Open a window. 2. Put one heap of soil in an old kadai on a medium flame. 3. Stir for 15 minutes, until the soil is dry and too hot to touch all through. 4. Let it cool for 30 minutes. 5. Fill one cup with plain soil and one with roasted soil. 6. Label them and give each 3 tablespoons of water.
flow.say: Heat kills seeds, as cooking kills a grain of rice. Now one pot has living seeds and one does not. What do you guess for day 21? Why?
flow.kid: A grown-up roasts one heap. Fill two pots and label them. Water both. Write your guess and your reason.

ask.q: If plants grow in the roasted pot, where could they have come from?
good: Seeds blown in on the wind.
A seed that the heat missed.
Seeds carried by ants or dropped by a bird.

flow.parent: Roasting also kills most fungi and bacteria in the soil and changes its smell. Say so if your child asks. The difference you will see is mostly about seeds.
flow.context: This step of The Soil Remembers is the roasting. A grown-up heats one heap of soil to kill the seeds in it.

flow.do: 1. Keep both pots on the same bright sill. 2. Give each 2 tablespoons of water a day, so the soil stays damp. 3. On days 4, 7, 14 and 21, count the plants in each pot and fill in the table.
flow.say: Count carefully. What do you notice about the two pots today? Is anything growing that is not a plant with leaves?
flow.kid: Water both pots the same. Count the plants on days 4, 7, 14 and 21. Fill in the table.
flow.parent: The plain pot usually shows its first seedlings between day 4 and day 10. If neither pot has any by day 14, the soil had few seeds. That is a result too. Start again with soil from a weedier place.
flow.context: This step of The Soil Remembers is the watching. You count the plants in both pots four times in three weeks.

flow.do: 1. Count both pots for the last time. 2. Draw each pot from above. 3. Ask for the claim, the evidence and the reason. 4. Only then give the explanation below.
flow.say: What do you think is true about where new plants come from? Which numbers show it? Why did the two pots differ? Then I will tell you the scientists' words.
flow.kid: Count both pots. Where do new plants come from? Which numbers show it? Say why the pots differ.

check.q: A forest burns, but the soil is not badly heated. Where will most of the first new plants come from?
options: From seeds and roots already in the soil
From nowhere, so it stays bare
Only from seeds blown from far away
check.why: Soil holds a seed bank and living roots, so plants appear within weeks. This is secondary succession. Choosing 'only from far away' describes primary succession, as on new lava, which is much slower.

flow.parent: After your child has answered, explain: the plain pot started with a seed bank, like land after a fire or a storm. That is secondary succession. The roasted pot is like new lava. Every plant there had to arrive from outside, which is primary succession.
flow.context: This is the last step of The Soil Remembers. Here you compare the two pots and explain the difference.

activities.title: Nobody Planted Me: who settles a bare place first?
activities.context: In this activity you look for plants that are growing where nobody planted them, on walls, in cracks and in old pots. You work out how each one got there. They are the first step of the change this unit is about.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a magnifying glass, if you have one

activities.record: Draw or list five plants nobody planted. Beside each, write where the plant is growing, what the roots are holding on to, and how you think the seed or spore arrived.

setup.art: A child on an apartment staircase pointing at a small fern growing from a crack where a pipe drips down a wall.
setup.caption: 1. Look on walls, in cracks, under dripping pipes and in old plant pots.

setup.art: A notebook page with five small sketches of plants, each with a note such as 'wall crack, came by bird'.
setup.caption: 2. For each plant, note where they grow and how the seed could have arrived.

setup.art: Two sketches side by side: moss on a bare wall labelled 'no soil', and weeds in a pot labelled 'soil was there'.
setup.caption: 3. Sort your plants: started with no soil, or started in soil that was already there.

flow.do: 1. Ask how many plants that nobody planted can be found within 30 steps of your front door. 2. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.say: How many plants that nobody planted are within 30 steps of our door? Where do you expect to find them? Why there?
flow.kid: Guess how many unplanted plants are near your door. Where will they be? Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Nobody Planted Me. Here you guess before you look.

flow.do: 1. Look in your own plant pots first, for any plant you did not sow. 2. Look at the balcony, the stairs, the compound wall and the ground by the gate. 3. Find five. 4. For each, look at what the roots hold on to.
flow.say: Look at this one. What are the roots holding? Is there any soil? How could a seed have reached this spot?
flow.kid: Find five plants nobody planted. Look at their roots. How did each seed get there?

ask.q: How could a seed reach a crack high on a wall?
good: A bird ate a fruit and left the seed in a dropping.
The wind carried it.
Moss and ferns come from spores, which are like dust and float in the air.

flow.parent: In a flat with no way out, the pots on a balcony and the view from a window are enough. Green film or moss on a damp wall counts. Peepal and banyan seedlings on walls come from seeds in bird droppings.
flow.context: This is the main step of Nobody Planted Me. Here you find five plants that nobody planted.

flow.do: 1. Sort the five into two groups: started with no soil, and started in soil. 2. Choose one plant. 3. Ask what that spot would look like in 50 years if nobody touched it.
flow.say: Which of these started with no soil at all? Now choose one. If nobody touches that spot for 50 years, what will be there? Why?
flow.kid: Sort your plants: no soil, or soil already there. Choose one. What will be there in 50 years?
flow.think: A peepal seedling in a wall crack can become a tree that splits the wall. Who is stronger, the wall or the seed?
flow.context: This is the last step of Nobody Planted Me. Here you sort your finds and think 50 years ahead.

activities.title: The Wolf Chain: what is counted, what is argued, what is claimed too much?
activities.context: In this activity you sort eight claims about the wolves who were brought back to Yellowstone National Park in 1995. Some are counted and agreed. Some are argued about by scientists. Some claim more than the evidence shows. Then you draw the chain with solid and dotted arrows.

materials.item: paper cut into 8 slips, and a pen
a large sheet of paper for the chain
two colour pencils

activities.record: Draw the chain from wolves to rivers. Use a solid arrow where the link is counted and agreed, and a dotted arrow where it is argued about. Cross out any link that claims too much.

example_chart.title: The eight claims and how scientists rate them today
rows: Wolves were brought back to Yellowstone in 1995 and 1996.
Elk on the northern range fell by more than half after 1995.
Wolves were the only reason the elk fell.
In some places, young aspen and willow have grown taller since the 1990s.
Elk keep away from valleys out of fear of wolves, and that let the trees grow.
Beaver colonies on the northern range rose from 1 to 9 between 2001 and 2011.
Willows have recovered along all the streams.
Wolves changed the course of the rivers.

setup.art: Eight paper slips with short sentences on them spread on a table, and three paper labels: 'counted and agreed', 'argued about', 'claims too much'.
setup.caption: 1. Copy the eight claims on slips. Make three labels.

setup.art: A child placing a slip under the label 'argued about' while an adult reads from a phone.
setup.caption: 2. Sort each claim under a label. Then check with the table.

setup.art: A drawn chain of boxes: wolf, elk, willow, beaver, river, joined by some solid arrows and some dotted arrows.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the chain. Solid arrows are agreed. Dotted arrows are argued about.

flow.do: 1. Read aloud the card 'The wolves of Yellowstone: what happened'. 2. Copy the eight claims from the table on eight slips. Do not copy the ratings. 3. Make three labels.
flow.say: Wolves were gone from this park for 70 years and then brought back. Here are eight things people say happened next.
flow.kid: Listen to the wolf story. Copy the eight claims on slips. Make three labels.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Wolf Chain. Here you hear the story and copy the eight claims.

flow.do: 1. Take one slip at a time. 2. Ask how anyone could know this, and what would have to be counted or measured. 3. Place it under a label. 4. When all eight are placed, check with the table.
flow.say: How could anyone know this? What would they have to count or measure? Could something else have caused it? Where does it go, and why?
flow.kid: Take a slip. How could anyone know this? Could something else cause it? Put it under a label.

ask.q: Elk fell after wolves came back. Why is that not proof that wolves did it all?
good: Other things changed in the same years.
Hunters, bears and cougars also killed elk, and there were dry years.
Two things happening together does not show that one caused the other.

flow.parent: Do not hurry to the table. The thinking is in the question 'could something else have caused it?'
flow.context: This is the main step of The Wolf Chain. Here you sort the claims by how strong the evidence is.

flow.do: 1. Draw boxes for wolf, elk, willow and aspen, beaver, and river. 2. Join them with solid arrows where the link is agreed and dotted arrows where it is argued. 3. Choose one dotted arrow and ask how it could be tested.
flow.say: Choose one dotted arrow. If you were a scientist in Yellowstone, what would you measure to settle it? Why would that settle it?
flow.kid: Draw the chain with solid and dotted arrows. Choose one dotted arrow. How could you test it?

check.q: Why is it hard to prove what the wolves changed in Yellowstone?
options: There is only one Yellowstone, and much else changed too
Scientists do not go there in winter
check.why: A fair test changes one thing and keeps a second copy unchanged. There is no second Yellowstone, and hunters, bears, cougars and weather changed in the same years. Choosing 'nobody has counted' is not right, because wolves and elk are counted every year.

flow.parent: Good tests: fence some willows from elk and compare. Raise the water with a small dam on some streams. Put collars on elk to see where they really go. Scientists have done all three.
flow.context: This is the last step of The Wolf Chain. Here you draw the chain and plan a test for one argued link.

activities.title: Wetland on a Board: what does a marsh do in a flood?
activities.context: In this activity a tilted board is a piece of land, a folded towel is a wetland, and a tumbler of water is a burst of rain. You measure how much water rushes off the land with the wetland, without it, and with the wetland built over.

materials.item: a chopping board or a flat steel tray, about 30 centimetres long
two books to prop up one end
a wide basin or parat to catch the water
a dry cotton hand towel
a steel tumbler of about 200 millilitres
a plastic carry bag, cut open flat
a watch or phone that shows seconds

activities.safety: Do this in the bathroom or beside the kitchen sink. Wipe the floor afterwards, because a wet floor is slippery.
activities.record: Make a table with four rows: bare board, dry towel, soaked towel, and towel under plastic. For each, write how much water reached the basin in 30 seconds: none, a quarter, half, or nearly all of the tumbler.

setup.art: A chopping board propped on two books at one end, with its low end resting over a wide steel basin.
setup.caption: 1. Prop one end of the board on two books. Put the low end over a basin.

setup.art: A folded hand towel lying across the middle of the tilted board from edge to edge, and a hand pouring a tumbler of water at the top.
setup.caption: 2. Lay a folded dry towel across the board. Pour one tumbler of water at the top.

setup.art: The same board with a plastic sheet laid over the towel and water running straight over the plastic into the basin.
setup.caption: 3. Cover the towel with plastic and pour again. Compare the water in the basin each time.

flow.do: 1. Prop the board on two books with the low end over the basin. 2. Pour one full tumbler along the top edge in about 5 seconds. 3. Wait 30 seconds. 4. Pour the water from the basin back into the tumbler and see how full it is.
flow.say: This board is land with no wetland. How much of the rain reached the bottom in 30 seconds? Now guess for a board with a towel across it. Why?
flow.kid: Pour one tumbler on the bare board. Wait 30 seconds. How much reached the basin? Guess for the towel.
flow.parent: Nearly the whole tumbler reaches the basin within a few seconds.
flow.context: This is the first step of Wetland on a Board. Here you pour rain on bare land and measure what runs off.

flow.do: 1. Empty the basin. 2. Fold the dry towel in four and lay it across the middle of the board, from edge to edge. 3. Pour one tumbler at the top and wait 30 seconds. Measure the basin. 4. Pour a second and a third tumbler, measuring after each. 5. Then watch the low edge of the towel for two minutes.
flow.say: What happened to the first tumbler? What changed with the second and third? What is the towel doing now that the rain has stopped?
flow.kid: Lay the towel across the board. Pour three tumblers, one by one. Measure each time. Then watch for drips.

ask.q: What do you notice after the rain has stopped?
good: The towel keeps dripping slowly for a long time.
The first tumbler was held, but later ones ran through.
A full towel cannot hold more.

flow.parent: A dry folded hand towel usually holds all of the first tumbler and much of the second. By the third, most of the water runs through. That is real too: a marsh that is already full cannot stop a second storm.
flow.context: This is the main step of Wetland on a Board. Here a dry towel plays the wetland, and you pour three bursts of rain.

flow.do: 1. Lay the plastic sheet over the wet towel. 2. Pour one tumbler at the top and measure after 30 seconds. 3. Ask for the claim, the evidence and the reason. 4. Then read the explanation card on rivers and wetlands.
flow.say: The plastic is a road and buildings on top of the marsh. What happened to the rain this time? What do you think a wetland does for a city? Which result shows it?
flow.kid: Cover the towel with plastic. Pour again and measure. What does a wetland do for a city? Which result shows it?

check.q: A marsh beside a city is filled in and built over. What changes when heavy rain falls?
options: Less rain falls on the city
Rain water reaches the streets faster
check.why: A marsh soaks up a rush of water and lets it out slowly, as the dry towel did. Built over, the water runs straight off, as it did over the plastic. Choosing 'less rain falls' mixes up how much rain falls with where it goes.

flow.context: This is the last step of Wetland on a Board. Here the wetland is built over, and you explain what you saw.

activities.title: Patchwork From Above: map the patches around your home
activities.context: In this activity you draw the land around your home as seen from above, and colour each patch by its kind. You find out how many kinds of patch there are, which are young and which are old, and whether the green ones join up.

materials.item: a sheet of plain paper and a pencil
colour pencils or crayons: grey, dark green, light green, blue, yellow and brown
a view from a terrace or high window, or the satellite view on a phone map

activities.safety: A grown-up comes to the terrace. Stay away from the edge.
activities.record: Keep the coloured map. Under it write how many patches of each kind you found, which green patch is the biggest, and one pair of green patches that an animal could not easily travel between.

setup.art: A child and an adult on a terrace looking out over rooftops, trees, an empty plot and a small lake.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the land around your home from high up, or on a satellite map.

setup.art: A hand-drawn map with outlined shapes being coloured: grey for buildings, dark green for trees, light green for weedy plots, blue for water.
setup.caption: 2. Draw each patch as a shape. Colour each by its kind.

setup.art: The finished map with a dotted line drawn along a row of street trees joining two green patches.
setup.caption: 3. Find the biggest green patch. Look for green paths that join one patch to another.

flow.do: 1. Go to the terrace or a high window. If you cannot, open the satellite view of a map around your home. 2. Ask how many kinds of patch the child expects, and which kind will cover the most land.
flow.say: From up here the land is a patchwork. How many kinds of patch do you think we will find? Which kind covers the most? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the land from above. How many kinds of patch can you see? Which covers the most?
flow.context: This is the first step of Patchwork From Above. Here you choose your view and guess what you will find.

flow.do: 1. Draw your building in the middle of the page. 2. Draw the patches around it as shapes. 3. Colour buildings and roads grey, big trees dark green, and weedy plots and grass light green. 4. Colour water blue, fields yellow and bare ground brown. 5. Mark each green patch Y for young or O for old.
flow.say: Is this patch young or old? How can you tell? What would have to happen for it to become old?
flow.kid: Draw your building. Draw the patches round it. Colour each kind. Mark green patches young or old.

ask.q: How can you tell a young patch from an old one?
good: An empty plot with weeds and small bushes is young.
Very big trees with thick trunks mean an old patch.
A patch cleared last year has no tall plants.

flow.parent: The map need not be to scale. A temple grove, an old campus or a line of big rain trees is usually the oldest patch in a city.
flow.context: This is the main step of Patchwork From Above. Here you draw and colour the map.

flow.do: 1. Count the patches of each colour. 2. Find the biggest green patch. 3. Choose two green patches and ask how a squirrel, a butterfly and a frog could travel between them. 4. Draw the best path as a dotted line.
flow.say: Could a squirrel get from this patch to that one? Could a frog? What is in the way? What one change would join them?
flow.kid: Count each colour. Could a squirrel cross between two green patches? Could a frog? Draw the best path.
flow.think: Your map shows one day. If you drew the same map in 30 years, which patches would have changed kind?
flow.context: This is the last step of Patchwork From Above. Here you read your map the way an animal would.

activities.title: The Hundred-Year Film: draw one place changing
activities.context: In this activity you draw the same piece of land five times, as it would look 0, 1, 10, 30 and 100 years after being cleared. You show who lives there at each time, and what each group changed for the next.

materials.item: a long strip of paper, or a sheet folded into five panels
a pencil and colour pencils

activities.record: Keep the strip of five pictures. Under each picture write one sentence: who lives here now, and what they are changing.

setup.art: A sheet of paper folded into five panels, labelled along the top: 0 years, 1 year, 10 years, 30 years, 100 years.
setup.caption: 1. Fold a sheet into five panels. Label them 0, 1, 10, 30 and 100 years.

setup.art: The first two panels drawn: a bare ploughed field, then the same field covered in grasses and small flowers with a grasshopper.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the cleared land. Then draw who arrives first.

setup.art: All five panels drawn, the last showing tall trees with a hornbill, and arrows between panels with short notes.
setup.caption: 3. Finish all five. Between panels, write what changed for the next group.

flow.do: 1. Fold the paper into five panels and label them. 2. Choose a place: a paddy field no longer farmed, a burnt slope, or a landslide in the hills. 3. Decide whether the soil is still there.
flow.say: Choose a piece of land that has just been cleared. Is the soil still there? Why does that matter for what comes first?
flow.kid: Fold five panels and label them. Choose a cleared place. Is the soil still there?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Hundred-Year Film. Here you choose your place and get the strip ready.

flow.do: 1. Draw the bare land in panel 1. 2. In each next panel, draw the plants and at least one animal that would live there by then. 3. Between panels, write what the earlier group changed: shade, soil, perches, or damp air.
flow.say: Who comes next? What do they need that was not here before? Who made it?
flow.kid: Draw each panel. Add plants and one animal. Write what changed between panels.

ask.q: Why can the trees of panel 5 not simply grow in panel 2?
good: Their seedlings need shade and damp soil.
Their seeds have not arrived yet, because no birds are visiting.
The soil is still too poor and dry.

flow.parent: There is no single right film. Grass, then shrubs, then sun-loving trees, then shade-bearing trees is the usual order where rain is good. In a dry place the film may end in scrub or grassland.
flow.context: This is the main step of The Hundred-Year Film. Here you draw the five pictures.

flow.do: 1. Choose one panel. 2. Draw a small storm cloud above it. 3. Ask what the next panel would show now, and draw it on the back.
flow.say: A cyclone hits your place at this panel. Does the film go back to the start? What is left that helps it recover? Why?
flow.kid: A storm hits one panel. Does the film start again? What is left? Draw what comes next.

check.q: A storm fells the trees of a 30-year-old forest. The soil stays. How does it regrow, compared with bare rock?
check.why: The soil still holds seeds, roots, fungi and water, so plants return within weeks. Bare rock must first gain soil. Choosing 'the same speed' treats every disturbance as a start from nothing.

flow.context: This is the last step of The Hundred-Year Film. Here a storm strikes your film.

projects.title: A Healing Plan for One Real Place
projects.context: In this five-day project you choose one damaged place near your home, such as an empty plot, a dirty pond or a bare road edge. You find out what it used to be and what is stopping it from recovering. Then you write a plan a real restorer could use.

materials.item: a notebook, a pencil and colour pencils
a large sheet of paper for the final plan
an older neighbour or relative to interview
a phone camera, if you have one

projects.safety: A grown-up comes with you to the place. Do not go into water, rubbish or thick bushes.

schedule.what: Choose the place, visit it and draw a map of it.
Ask an older person what the place used to be. Look for a healthy place of the same kind.
List what is blocking the place from recovering.
Write the plan: three actions, in order, and who must agree to each.
Present the plan to your family and answer their questions.

projects.record: The final sheet has four parts: a map of the place today, a drawing of what it could become, a list of what blocks it, and three actions in order with the name of who must agree to each.

setup.art: A child and an adult standing at the edge of a weedy empty plot with a small pond, the child sketching a map.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one damaged place nearby. Visit it and draw a map.

setup.art: A child with a notebook listening to an elderly woman who is pointing across a street.
setup.caption: 2. Ask an older person what the place was like long ago.

setup.art: A large sheet with a map, a drawing, a list headed 'what blocks it' and three numbered actions.
setup.caption: 3. List what blocks recovery. Write three actions and who must agree.

flow.do: 1. Choose a place you can visit safely. 2. Walk round its edge. 3. Draw a map with its patches: bare ground, weeds, trees, water, rubbish. 4. List every living being you see.
flow.say: What lives here already? What looks as if it is trying to grow back? What do you think this place used to be? Why?
flow.kid: Choose a damaged place. Draw a map of its patches. List who lives there already.
flow.parent: A small place is best: one empty plot, one stretch of drain, the edge of one tank. Something is nearly always growing back already, and that is the first clue.
flow.context: This is day 1 of A Healing Plan for One Real Place. Here you choose the place and map it.

flow.do: 1. Ask an older neighbour or relative what the place was like 30 or 50 years ago. 2. Write down what they say. 3. Look for a healthy place of the same kind nearby, as a reference site. 4. List three things the healthy place has that yours lacks.
flow.say: What was here before? Was it a field, a tank, a marsh, a grove or open grass? Which healthy place nearby is most like that?
flow.kid: Ask an older person what was here long ago. Find a healthy place like it. List three differences.
flow.parent: The answer may surprise you. Many empty plots in Indian cities were once tanks, marshes or grazing land, not forest.
flow.context: This is day 2 of A Healing Plan for One Real Place. Here you find out what the place used to be.

flow.do: 1. Look at your map and your notes. 2. Ask what kills or removes living beings here again and again. 3. Ask what the place needs that cannot reach it. 4. Write a list headed 'what blocks it'.
flow.say: Something stops this place from growing back. Is something being taken away again and again? Is something unable to arrive? What do you think, and why?
flow.kid: What keeps harming this place? What cannot reach it? Write a list of what blocks it.

ask.q: What kinds of thing can block recovery?
good: Grazing, burning, trampling or dumping that keeps happening.
Water that no longer flows in or out.
No seeds, because the nearest healthy place is far away.
Weeds that cover everything.

flow.context: This is day 3 of A Healing Plan for One Real Place. Here you find what blocks the place from recovering.

flow.do: 1. Choose the three most useful actions. 2. Put them in order, with the removal of a block first. 3. Beside each, write who must agree: neighbours, the owner, the ward office. 4. Draw what the place could look like in ten years.
flow.say: Which block would you remove first? What will the place do by itself after that? What must people still bring?
flow.kid: Choose three actions. Put them in order. Write who must agree. Draw the place in ten years.
flow.parent: A good plan removes a block before it adds anything. Planting comes last, and only what the reference site shows belongs there.
flow.context: This is day 4 of A Healing Plan for One Real Place. Here you write the plan.

flow.do: 1. Put the final sheet on a wall. 2. Present it in three minutes. 3. Let each listener ask one question. 4. Ask what could go wrong with the plan.
flow.say: Tell us your plan. Then tell us one thing that could go wrong, and how you would find out early.
flow.kid: Present your plan in three minutes. Answer one question each. Say what could go wrong.

check.q: What is the best first step in restoring a damaged place?
options: Find out what blocks its recovery
check.why: Most places are trying to regrow all the time. Removing the block lets that happen. Choosing 'plant fast-growing trees' skips the question of what the place was and why it is not recovering.

flow.context: This is day 5 of A Healing Plan for One Real Place. Here you present your plan.

challenges.title: The Seed Ball Drop: a ball that lands whole and still sprouts
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about seed balls. A seed ball is a small ball of soil with seeds inside, made to be thrown onto bare land. You design a ball that survives a fall and still lets its seeds sprout.
challenges.problem: Make a seed ball that does not break when dropped from one metre onto the floor. Its seeds must still sprout within seven days once the ball is wetted.
constraints: Use only soil, clay or multani mitti, compost or dry cow dung, water and seeds.
Each ball holds exactly 10 methi or mustard seeds and is no bigger than a lemon.
Dry the balls in the shade for one day before the drop test.
After the drop, keep the balls on a damp plate. You may not break them open.
materials: clay, or multani mitti from a general shop, about half a tumbler
compost or crumbled dry cow dung, about 1 tumbler
a plate, a spoon and water
a ruler or tape to mark one metre
general: A ball made mostly of clay. It lands whole, but it dries as hard as a brick.
A ball made mostly of compost. Seeds sprout easily, but it crumbles when dropped.
A large ball with the seeds mixed all through.
creative: Put the seeds in a soft compost middle and wrap a thin clay skin round it.
Mix in chopped dry grass or coconut fibre, which holds the ball together the way straw holds a mud wall.
Press the ball into a flat disc, so that it lands without rolling and the seeds lie near the surface.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own ball. Draw it cut in half and label what is where. Make it, drop it, wet it and count the sprouts on day 7. What would you change next time?

setup.art: Three small heaps on a newspaper labelled soil, clay and compost, a saucer of seeds and a child rolling a ball of mud between her palms.
setup.caption: 1. Mix your recipe. Roll three balls, each with 10 seeds.

setup.art: A child holding a dried mud ball at the one-metre mark on a ruler taped to a wall, about to drop it.
setup.caption: 2. After one day of drying, drop each ball from one metre.

setup.art: Three mud balls on a wet plate, one cracked in half, one whole with tiny green sprouts coming out of it.
setup.caption: 3. Keep the balls damp for seven days. Count the sprouts.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem and the rules together. 2. Ask what makes a ball strong, and what a seed inside needs. 3. Ask whether those two pull in opposite ways.
flow.say: The ball must be tough enough to land and soft enough for a root to push out. What would make it tough? What would make it soft? Why?
flow.kid: A ball must land whole and still sprout. What makes it strong? What does a seed need?

ask.q: What does a seed inside the ball need in order to sprout?
good: Water reaching the seed.
Air.
A skin thin or soft enough for the root and shoot to push through.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Seed Ball Drop. Here you think about the two things the ball must do.

flow.do: 1. Make three balls with three different recipes. 2. Put exactly 10 seeds in each. 3. Write each recipe in spoonfuls. 4. Leave the balls in the shade for one day.
flow.say: Change one thing between each ball and the next, so we can tell what made the difference.
flow.kid: Make three balls with different recipes. Put 10 seeds in each. Write down each recipe.
flow.wait: Leave the balls to dry for 1 day
flow.parent: Add water a spoonful at a time, until the mix holds together like chapati dough. Wash hands afterwards.
flow.context: This is the making step of the Seed Ball Drop. Here you make three different designs.

flow.do: 1. Mark one metre on a wall. 2. Drop each ball once onto the floor from that height. 3. Note whether it stayed whole, cracked or broke up. 4. Put all three on a plate and pour on 4 tablespoons of water. 5. Keep the plate damp for 7 days.
flow.say: Which ball landed best? Which do you think will sprout best? Are they the same ball? Why?
flow.kid: Drop each ball from one metre. Note what happened. Put them on a wet plate.
flow.wait: Keep the plate damp for 7 days
flow.context: This is the testing step of the Seed Ball Drop. Here you drop the balls and start them growing.

flow.do: 1. Count the sprouts on each ball. 2. Write the score: sprouts out of 10, and whole or broken. 3. Read the usual and the creative ideas above. 4. Ask what the child would change.
flow.say: Which design did both jobs best? What would you change? Would a seed ball be enough to restore a bare hill? Why?
flow.kid: Count the sprouts on each ball. Which design did both jobs? What would you change?

check.q: Seed balls are thrown onto a bare, dry hill. What decides most whether trees grow there?
options: Whether the hill's blocks to recovery are gone
check.why: A sprouted seed still needs water, soil and safety from grazing and fire. If those blocks remain, most seedlings die. Choosing 'how many balls' treats a shortage of seeds as the only problem.

flow.parent: Be honest about seed balls. They are popular in India, but there are few careful counts of how many thrown seeds become trees. Many are eaten, or sprout and dry out.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Seed Ball Drop. Here you count the sprouts and judge the designs.

challenges.title: Plan the Patchwork: farms, homes and wild land on one grid
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about sharing land. A grid of 36 squares is a village's land, with a river along its left edge. You must fit in farms and homes, and still leave wild patches that work for the living beings who need them.
challenges.problem: Fill a grid of 6 by 6 squares with farms, homes, forest, wetland and grassland, so that every rule below is kept.
constraints: The river runs along the left edge of the grid. Hills with forest lie beyond the top edge and beyond the bottom edge.
The village needs 16 farm squares and 6 home squares.
At least 4 squares are wetland, and each wetland square is in the left column, beside the river.
At least 2 squares are grassland for grazing.
The forest squares touch each other side to side in one unbroken piece. That piece reaches both the top edge and the bottom edge.
No home square shares a side with a wetland square, because wetlands flood.
materials: squared paper, or a grid of 6 by 6 squares drawn with a ruler
colour pencils: yellow for farms, red for homes, dark green for forest, blue for wetland, light green for grassland
general: Put the forest as one straight strip from top to bottom, six squares long.
Put the homes in the right column, far from the river.
Fill everything left over with farms.
creative: Run the forest strip next to the wetland along the river. Trees on a river bank hold the soil and shade the water.
Use the two spare squares to make the forest strip two squares wide at one point, as a resting place for animals.
Put the grassland between the forest and the farms, so that deer and pigs meet grass before they meet crops.
challenges.your_turn: Now make your own plan and colour it. Then test it: put a finger on the top edge and walk it to the bottom edge through forest squares only. Which living beings does your plan suit best? Who does it suit least?

setup.art: A grid of 6 by 6 squares with a blue wavy line down its left side and small drawn hills above and below it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a grid of 36 squares. Draw the river along the left edge.

setup.art: The grid partly coloured: four blue squares by the river, a dark green strip from top to bottom, red squares on the right.
setup.caption: 2. Colour in wetland, forest, grassland, homes and farms. Keep every rule.

setup.art: A finger tracing a path down the dark green strip from the top edge to the bottom edge of the coloured grid.
setup.caption: 3. Test it: walk a finger from top to bottom through forest squares only.

flow.do: 1. Draw the grid and the river. 2. Read the six rules aloud. 3. Add up the squares the rules demand, and find how many are spare.
flow.say: The rules ask for farms, homes, wetland, grassland and a forest strip. How many squares is that at least? How many are spare? What will you do with them?
flow.kid: Draw the grid and the river. Read the rules. How many squares do the rules use up?
flow.parent: The least is 16 farms, 6 homes, 4 wetland, 2 grassland and 6 forest, which makes 34. So 2 squares are spare.
flow.context: This is the first step of Plan the Patchwork. Here you read the rules and count the squares.

flow.do: 1. Mark the plan lightly in pencil first. 2. Check each rule in turn. 3. Colour the squares. 4. Decide what the two spare squares will be, and why.
flow.say: Which rule was hardest to keep? What did you choose for the spare squares? Why?
flow.kid: Plan in pencil first. Check every rule. Then colour. Choose what the spare squares will be.

ask.q: Why must the forest be one unbroken piece from top to bottom?
good: So that animals can walk between the two hill forests without crossing farms.
Separate forest squares are too small for many animals.
Seeds and animals can move along it.

flow.context: This is the main step of Plan the Patchwork. Here you make and colour your plan.

flow.do: 1. Walk a finger from the top edge to the bottom edge through forest squares only. 2. Check that no home touches a wetland. 3. Read the usual and the creative ideas above. 4. Ask what the child would change.
flow.say: Your plan keeps the rules. Now, who is it best for? Who would complain about it: a farmer, an elephant, a frog? Why?
flow.kid: Test your plan with a finger. Who is it best for? Who would complain? Say why.

check.q: Two plans have the same number of forest squares. In one they are joined, in the other scattered. Which suits forest animals better?
check.why: Joined forest lets animals and seeds move, and has less edge. Scattered squares are each too small for many beings. Choosing 'both the same' counts area only and forgets how the patches are arranged.

flow.context: This is the last step of Plan the Patchwork. Here you test your plan and compare it with other ideas.

items.p: What is a disturbance?
items.why: A disturbance clears living beings from a place quickly: a storm, a fire, a flood, a bulldozer. Choosing 'a noisy animal' uses the everyday meaning of the word.
opts: An event that removes many living beings quickly

items.p: The first living beings to settle on bare ground are called ____ species.
items.why: Pioneers arrive easily and can live in the open. Lichens, mosses and grasses are common pioneers.

items.p: Put these in the order they usually appear on an abandoned field.
items.why: Each group changes the place for the next. Grasses hold the soil. Shrubs give shade and perches. Sun-loving trees make the shade that slower trees' seedlings can bear.

items.p: Why do pioneer plants not keep a patch for ever?
items.why: Pioneers change the place. Their own seedlings need full sun and do badly in the shade the pioneers made. Choosing 'they are weak' is not right: they are the only ones able to start on bare ground.
opts: Their seedlings grow badly in the shade they make

items.p: True or false: after a forest fire, new plants must wait for seeds to blow in from far away.
items.why: False. The soil usually still holds seeds and living roots, so plants return within weeks. This is secondary succession.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.why: These are the main words of the unit. A strong answer could give an example of each.
pairs: starting on ground with no soil and no life
starting where the soil is still there
living seeds waiting in the soil
many patches of different ages side by side
people helping a damaged place recover

items.p: In The Soil Remembers, plants came up in a pot where nothing was planted. Where did they come from?
items.a: From seeds that were already in the soil, called the seed bank. In the roasted pot the heat had killed them, so few or no plants grew.
items.why: A strong answer names the seed bank and uses the roasted pot as the evidence.

items.p: Sort each start into primary or secondary succession.
items.why: Primary starts with no soil. Secondary starts with the soil, its seeds and its roots still there.
items: a paddy field no longer farmed
a new island of ash in the sea
a forest gap after a cyclone
bare rock left by a melting glacier

items.p: In the Patchwork Test, why did the old forest count stop falling?
items.why: About as many patches grew old each round as were cleared, so the count stayed level. Choosing 'the storms stopped' is not right: 6 storms came in every round.
opts: The dice ran out of squares

items.p: Draw a forest from above as a patchwork. Show patches of four ages and label each one.
items.a: A map-like drawing with at least four patches labelled, for example, bare, grass, young trees and old forest.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the ages side by side in one landscape. A drawing of one even forest has missed the idea of a patchwork.
items.art: An empty outline of a forest seen from above.

items.p: True or false: wolves were brought back to Yellowstone National Park in 1995 and 1996.
items.why: True. 14 wolves came in 1995 and 17 in 1996, all caught in Canada. The last Yellowstone wolves had been killed in 1926.

items.p: At Pichavaram, what was killing the mangrove seedlings on the sunken ground?
items.why: Sea water stood still there and dried in the sun, so the salt built up. Channels let the tide flow in and out again. Choosing 'too few seeds' is the mistake the planters first made.
opts: Standing water that had become too salty

items.p: A marsh soaks up flood water and lets it out ____.
items.why: A wetland holds a rush of water and releases it over hours or days, as the towel did in Wetland on a Board.

items.p: Why is planting trees on a natural grassland not restoration?
items.a: Because the grassland is the ecosystem that belongs there. The grasses, blackbuck, larks and bustards need open country. Trees replace their home with a plantation.
items.why: A strong answer says that restoration aims at what the place naturally is, and that a grassland is not damaged forest.

items.p: What should a restorer ask first about a damaged place?
items.why: Most places regrow by themselves once the block is gone. Choosing 'how many trees can I plant' assumes the problem is always a lack of trees.
opts: How many trees can I plant?
What is stopping this place from recovering?
How can I make it tidy?

items.p: A Patchwork Test round has 6 bare, 5 grass and 4 young patches. How many of the 36 are old?
items.why: Add the three: 6 + 5 + 4 = 15. Then 36 − 15 = 21 old patches.

items.p: With 12 storms a round, not 6, what happened to the old forest count?
items.why: It settled at about 13, down from about 22. It still levelled off. Choosing 'zero' forgets that some patches always escape for three rounds.
opts: It levelled off at a lower number

items.p: After 60 storms on 36 patches, more than half the forest was still old. How can that be?
items.a: Storms fall on patches at random, so many hit bare or young patches that had been hit before. Meanwhile every patch that escapes for three rounds becomes old again.
items.why: A strong answer has both parts: storms overlap, and patches regrow. An answer that says 'the storms missed' has only the first part.

items.p: Lupines can grow on bare volcanic ash because bacteria in their roots take ____ from the air.
items.why: Plants need nitrogen to build their bodies. New ash has almost none that a plant can use, so plants with these bacteria get a head start.

items.p: Sort each being into the stage where you would expect to find them.
items.why: Pioneers travel light and need sun. Old forest beings need what only time gives: huge trees, a closed canopy and damp shade.
items: Macaranga tree in a sunny gap

items.p: On the new island of Surtsey, where did plants grow thickest?
items.why: Seabird droppings carry nitrogen and other plant food from the sea to the land. Choosing 'the highest point' forgets that new rock has almost no plant food.

items.p: Elk fell after wolves returned to Yellowstone. Give two other causes that could have lowered the elk.
items.a: Any two of: hunting by people outside the park, more grizzly bears, more cougars, and dry years.
items.why: A strong answer shows that several things changed in the same years, so the fall cannot be put down to wolves alone.

items.p: Two teams measured the same Yellowstone willows and disagreed. What did they do differently?
items.why: One team measured height and the other the volume of the leafy crown. What you choose to measure can change the answer. Choosing 'one team made up numbers' is not what happened.

items.p: Draw a stream with a beaver dam, and without one. Show the water level under the ground in both.
items.a: Two cut-away drawings. With the dam: a pond, water just under the bank, tall willows. Without: a deep narrow channel, water far below the bank, short willows.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the water under the ground at two different levels. That hidden water is why willows did not recover with wolves alone.
items.art: Two empty cut-away outlines of a stream bank, side by side.

items.p: Three of these remove a block to recovery. Which one does not?
items.why: Fencing, channels and dam removal each take away something that stops regrowth. Planting one kind of tree in rows adds a plantation and removes no block.
opts: Fencing cattle out of a regrowing field
Digging channels to let the tide in
Planting one kind of tree in rows

items.p: At Pichavaram, 375 hectares were damaged. Six years into the work, 65 were. How many hectares had recovered?
items.why: 375 − 65 = 310 hectares had young or grown mangroves again.

items.p: True or false: a forest restored 15 years ago is as rich as an old forest beside it.
items.why: False. In the Anamalai hills, restored fragments were ahead of unrestored ones but still behind the old forest. Big trees, nest holes and deep soil take far longer.

items.p: In Wetland on a Board, what did the third tumbler of water show?
items.why: A towel that is already full lets new water run through. A marsh works the same way. Choosing 'wetlands stop all floods' claims too much.
opts: A full wetland cannot hold more

items.p: Three people look at a bare, grazed hillside next to a forest.
items.a: A strong answer picks a view and uses the idea of a block to recovery. Seeds can arrive from the forest, so the block is grazing, and Lakshmi's fence may be enough. It can grant that planting helps where seeds cannot arrive.
items.why: All three want the hill green. They differ on what is stopping it now.

views.says: Plant ten thousand saplings in the monsoon. The more we plant, the faster it becomes forest.
Fence the goats out and wait. The forest next door will send the seeds.
First find out what this hill was. If it was grassland, leave it as grassland.

items.ask: Whose plan would you try first? Say what you think blocks this hill from recovering. Then give one fair point from another view.

items.p: Why did the forest in the Patchwork Test need storms for grasshoppers to live there?
items.a: Grasshoppers need grass patches. With no storms every patch became old forest, and there was no grass. Storms kept making new young patches.
items.why: A strong answer links the animal to a stage, and the stage to disturbance.

items.p: Every square in the Patchwork Test changed, yet the old count stayed near 22. How can both be true?
items.a: Each round some old squares were cleared and some young squares grew old. The squares swapped roles, but the numbers lost and gained were about equal, so the total stayed level.
items.why: A strong answer separates the single patch, which keeps changing, from the whole mix, which stays steady.

items.p: Six storms hit 6 different patches out of 36. What is the chance, in sixths, that one named patch escapes?
items.why: 30 of the 36 patches escape. 30 out of 36 is the same as 5 out of 6. So the chance is 5 sixths.

items.p: A patch needs to escape storms three rounds running to become old. What is that chance, roughly?
items.why: 5/6 × 5/6 × 5/6 = 125/216, which is a little over one half. Choosing '5 in 6' forgets that the patch must escape three times, not once.

items.p: True or false: most ecologists today think every place moves to one fixed final community and then stops changing.
items.why: False. That was the climax idea of 1916. Old communities change slowly, but they keep changing as trees die, the climate shifts and species arrive.

items.p: After the ice age, each tree species spread north at a different speed. What does this say about forests?
items.a: That a forest is not one unit that moves together. Each species goes their own way, so the mix of trees in a place keeps being put together afresh.
items.why: A strong answer sees that this supports Gleason's view: a community is whoever lives together at the time.

items.p: Draw the Yellowstone chain: wolf, elk, willow, beaver, stream. Make agreed links solid arrows and argued links dotted.
items.a: Wolf to elk is solid (wolves kill elk). Elk to willow is solid (elk eat willow). Willow to beaver is solid (beavers need willow). 'Wolves made willows recover everywhere' and 'wolves changed the rivers' are dotted or crossed out.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the single links are well known. What is argued is how strongly the whole chain ran after 1995.
items.art: Five empty boxes in a row labelled wolf, elk, willow, beaver, stream.

items.p: Why did willows on many Yellowstone streams stay short even with fewer elk?
items.why: With beavers gone, streams had cut deep and the water under the ground had sunk below the willow roots. Choosing 'wolves eat willows' mixes up the links of the chain.
opts: The water under the ground had sunk too low

items.p: Put these steps in the order they happened on Yellowstone streams after wolves were removed.
a: Streams cut deeper and ground water sank
items.why: Each step caused the next. The last step then kept willows short by itself, which is why bringing wolves back did not simply undo it.
items: Streams cut deeper and ground water sank

items.p: A lake stays green after its sewage is cut back. Why might the water not turn clear again?
items.a: The green algae shade out the bottom plants. Without those plants the mud is stirred up and the tiny animals who eat algae lose their shelter. So the green state keeps itself going.
items.why: A strong answer says that the lake has switched to a new state that holds itself in place. Removing the first cause is then not enough.

items.p: Two people talk about a restored forest of young trees.
items.a: A strong answer can take either side with reasons. The same kinds of tree are back, and animals are returning. But huge trees, nest holes, deep soil and the beings who need them are still missing, so it is not yet the same.
items.why: This question has no single right answer. It asks what makes a forest the forest it is.

views.says: It has the same kinds of tree as before. It is the same forest, only younger.
A hornbill cannot nest in it. Until she can, it is a different place.

items.ask: Who do you agree with more? Give one thing the young forest has, and one thing only time can give it.

items.p: Pallikaranai marsh shrank from about 5,500 hectares to about 600. Roughly how many parts out of 9 are left?
items.why: 5,500 ÷ 600 is a little over 9. So about 1 part in 9 is left, and about 8 parts in 9 are gone.

items.p: Salmon passed the old Elwha dam sites within two years. Why do scientists still say recovery will take decades?
items.why: The river bed, the banks and the fish numbers all need many salmon generations to rebuild. Choosing 'the dams were rebuilt' is not right.
opts: River, banks and fish numbers rebuild slowly

items.p: Three of these are natural ecosystems of India that should not be planted with trees. Which one is not?
items.why: A cleared rainforest fragment was forest, so local trees belong there. Dry grassland, salt desert and high mountain grassland are natural open ecosystems.

items.p: A healthy place of the same kind, studied to guide a restoration, is called a ____ site.
items.why: A reference site shows which living beings belong and what the damaged place could become.

items.p: People, beavers and elephants all cause disturbance. Name one way human disturbance is different, and one way the same.
items.a: Same: all three clear patches and change who can live there. Different: people clear far larger areas, far more often, and often leave no soil or seeds behind, as under concrete.
items.why: A strong answer compares size, how often, and what is left behind. Those are the three ways disturbances differ.

quiz.p: Which of these is a disturbance?
quiz.why: A cyclone removes many living beings in a short time. The others are slow, everyday events.
opts: A tree growing a new leaf

quiz.p: Why do lichens and mosses come before trees on bare rock?
quiz.why: They need no soil, and they help to make the first soil. Choosing 'they are older kinds of life' explains nothing about this rock.
opts: They are older kinds of life

quiz.p: A landslide and a lava flow each clear a slope. Which regrows faster, and why?
quiz.why: A landslide scar keeps some soil and lies next to living forest. Lava leaves no soil and no seeds, so succession there is primary and slow.
opts: The landslide: some soil and seeds remain

quiz.p: You plant nothing in a pot of soil from under weeds, and water it. What is most likely to happen?

quiz.p: Storms hit a large forest at a steady rate for centuries. What is the forest like?
quiz.why: Patches are cleared and regrow all the time, so the forest holds every age at once, in a steady mix.

quiz.p: True or false: in a steady forest, each single patch stays the same.
quiz.why: False. Each patch keeps changing. Only the mix of young and old across the whole landscape stays about the same.

quiz.p: Which statement about the wolves of Yellowstone is well shown by counting?

quiz.p: A missing predator is brought back, but the streams do not recover. What is the most likely reason?

The plants forgot how to grow

quiz.p: Mangroves are dying where sea water stands still on sunken ground. What is the best plan?
quiz.why: The block is standing salty water. Channels bring back the tide's flow. This is what worked at Pichavaram.

Build a wall against the sea

quiz.p: A city fills in its marshes and builds on them. What is the likely result in heavy rain?
quiz.why: The marsh no longer soaks up the rush of water, so it reaches the streets quickly and in one burst.

quiz.p: A dry grassland with blackbuck is marked 'wasteland'. What would restore it?
quiz.why: An open grassland is a natural ecosystem. It needs protection from ploughing, building and tree planting, not a forest on top of it.

open_questions.q: How much of the change in Yellowstone was caused by the wolves?
open_questions.why_open: Two teams of scientists measure the same valleys and reach different answers. There is only one Yellowstone, so no fair test with and without wolves can be run.

open_questions.q: Can we tell in advance that an ecosystem is close to a tipping point?
open_questions.why_open: Some lakes have shown warning signs before switching, such as slower recovery from small upsets. Nobody yet knows whether such signs can be trusted in forests, reefs or grasslands.

open_questions.q: How long does a restored rainforest take to become like an old one, and does it ever?
open_questions.why_open: The oldest careful restoration projects are only a few decades old. A rainforest tree can live for centuries, so nobody has watched for long enough.

open_questions.q: When the climate is changing, should a place be restored to what it was, or to what will suit the future?
open_questions.why_open: Some trees that grew in a place a hundred years ago may not thrive there in a warmer century. Restorers argue about whether to copy the past or plan for the new climate.

open_questions.q: Does a middle amount of disturbance really keep the most kinds of living beings?
open_questions.why_open: Some studies find it and many do not. Scientists disagree about whether the idea needs repair or should be dropped.

maths.problem: In the Patchwork Test, 6 storms hit 6 different patches out of 36. What is the chance that one patch escapes for three rounds running? About how many of the 36 patches is that?
maths.answer: 125 out of 216, which is a little over half. That is about 21 patches.
maths.explain: In one round, 30 of 36 patches escape, which is 5 out of 6. For three rounds, multiply: 5/6 × 5/6 × 5/6 = 125/216. That is about 0.58. And 0.58 × 36 is about 21. So about 21 patches should be old at any time.
maths.context: This is about the Patchwork Test, where dice send 6 storms a round onto a paper forest of 36 patches. A patch is old when no storm has hit it for three rounds.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying chances lets you work out the answer before you roll, and then check it against your own count.

maths.problem: With 12 storms a round, the same sum gives 2/3 × 2/3 × 2/3 of 36, which is about 11 old patches. Real games give about 13. Why is the real number higher?
maths.answer: Because 12 storms do not hit 12 different patches. Some land on a patch already hit in that round, so fewer patches are cleared.
maths.explain: The sum assumes that 12 different patches are cleared each round, leaving 24 of 36, which is 2 out of 3. But dice repeat. With 12 rolls on 36 squares, about 10 different squares are hit on average. So more patches escape than the sum says, and more grow old.
maths.context: This is about part 2 of the Patchwork Test, where 12 storms a round hit a paper forest of 36 patches.
maths.why_maths: When a sum and a test disagree, the gap points to something the sum left out. Finding it is how models get better.

maths.problem: Look at the graph of old forest patches over 10 rounds. In which round did the count stop falling? How far does it wander after that?
maths.answer: It stopped falling in round 3. After that it stays between 21 and 22.
maths.explain: The count goes 36, 30, 26, 22, and then 21, 22, 21, 22, 22, 21, 22. The fall ends at round 3, because a patch cleared in round 1 first becomes old again in round 4. From then on, gains match losses.
maths.context: This is about the Patchwork Test. You count the old forest patches on a grid of 36 after each round of storms.

chart.title: Made-up example: old forest patches with 6 storms a round

maths.why_maths: A line graph shows at a glance where a number stops changing. That flat part is the steady state.

maths.problem: The winter count of elk on Yellowstone's northern range was 16,791 in 1995 and 8,335 in 2004. Did the elk fall by more than half, or by less?
maths.answer: By a little more than half.
maths.explain: Half of 16,791 is about 8,396. The 2004 count, 8,335, is a little below that. So the elk fell by slightly more than half in nine years.
maths.context: This is about the wolves brought back to Yellowstone National Park in 1995. Rangers count the elk there every winter.
maths.why_maths: Halving a big number in your head tells you quickly whether a claim such as 'fell by half' is fair.

maths.problem: At Pichavaram, 375 hectares of mangrove were damaged. Six years into the work, 65 hectares still were. About what fraction of the damaged area had recovered?
maths.answer: 310 out of 375, which is about 5 parts in every 6.
maths.explain: 375 − 65 = 310 hectares recovered. 375 ÷ 6 is about 62, and 5 × 62 = 310. So about 5 sixths recovered, which is about 83 in every 100.
maths.context: This is about the mangrove forest of Pichavaram in Tamil Nadu, where channels were dug from 1996 to let the tide back in.
maths.why_maths: A fraction tells you how complete a recovery is, which the bare number of hectares does not.

maths.problem: Pallikaranai marsh covered about 5,500 hectares in 1965 and about 600 hectares in 2013. About how many hectares were lost each year, on average?
maths.explain: 5,500 − 600 = 4,900 hectares lost. From 1965 to 2013 is 48 years. 4,900 ÷ 48 is about 102. So about 100 hectares went each year, which is 1 square kilometre a year.
maths.context: This is about Pallikaranai marsh in Chennai, a wetland that has been filled in and built over since the 1960s.
maths.why_maths: A slow loss is easy to miss from one year to the next. An average rate turns it into one number that you can picture.
