how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out what happens to a place after it is cleared? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out to be wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: In 1899 Henry Cowles walked inland from the shore of Lake Michigan in the United States. Near the water the sand dunes were bare. Further back, older dunes carried grass, then shrubs, then forest. He saw that walking inland was like walking forward in time. In 1916 Frederic Clements built a grand theory on this. He said a plant community is like one giant living being. It grows up through fixed stages to an adult form, the climax, and then stays. This idea filled textbooks for forty years. In 1926 Henry Gleason disagreed. He said each species spreads separately, wherever the seeds land and the plant finds what is needed. Almost nobody listened to him. In the 1950s Robert Whittaker and John Curtis measured real forests and found Gleason's pattern. Then Margaret Davis read the pollen buried in lake mud, layer by layer. She showed that after the ice age each kind of tree had moved north at a different speed, by a different path. The forests of today were never one being. They were put together, kind by kind.
how_we_found_out.who: Henry Cowles, Frederic Clements, Henry Gleason, Robert Whittaker, John Curtis and Margaret Davis, all in the United States.
how_we_found_out.when: 1899 (the dunes), 1916 (the climax theory), 1926 (Gleason's reply), the 1950s (the forest measurements) and the 1960s and 1970s (the pollen maps)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a community of plants is like one living being that grows up to a fixed adult form, the climax, and then stops changing. Measurements of real forests, and pollen in lake mud, showed that each species comes and goes separately and that communities keep changing.
how_we_found_out.art: A cut-away of lake mud in layers with tiny pollen grains in each layer, and above it a map with arrows of different lengths showing trees spreading north.

roots.context: We have learned how places are cleared, how they grow back, and how people help them heal. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Patchwork Test, storms cleared patches in every round, and no square stayed the same for long. Yet from round 3 the forest kept about 22 old patches. A forest does not stay the same by being left alone. It stays the same because patches fall and grow back at matching rates. So a healed place is one where falling and regrowing are in step again, even if it looks different from before.
deep_truth.habit: We think of a forest as a thing that stands still, and of damage as something done to it from outside. So we think healing means putting it back exactly as it was. But the forest was never still. What we call 'the forest' is a steady mix made by endless change.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Patchwork Test the old forest count stayed near 22 while every square changed. At Pichavaram the mangroves regrew once the tide flowed, without being put back tree by tree. In Yellowstone the wolves returned, and the streams still did not go back to what they had been.

three.who_am_i: Your skin, your blood and the lining of your gut are replaced again and again. You stay yourself because loss and regrowth keep step, as the patches did.
three.what_is_life: Life in a place is not a fixed list of beings. It is beings taking turns, each making room for others and then giving way.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is not a finished picture that gets damaged and repaired. It is always being cleared somewhere and always growing back somewhere.

roots.thread: A bare patch after a fire looks like nothing. But the soil is full of seeds, roots and spores, so the bare patch holds everything that could grow there. One lichen or one blade of grass arrives, and from that start come many kinds, each making room for the next. The young patch, the thicket and the old trees look like different things. They are one forest at different moments of the same change.

teachings.teaching: It is rain that ruins people, and it is rain again that lifts up those who were ruined.
teachings.link: Valluvar saw that the same thing can clear and restore. A flood strips a river bank, and the silt it leaves grows the next forest. At Pichavaram, standing sea water killed the mangroves and flowing sea water brought them back.

teachings.teaching: On those who step into the same rivers, different and again different waters flow.
teachings.link: The river stays the same river because its water keeps changing. The forest in the Patchwork Test stayed the same forest because its patches kept changing.

teachings.teaching: Everything that is put together from parts keeps changing. Seeing this clearly is the path to freedom from sorrow.
teachings.link: The Buddha taught this about all things. Ecologists found it of forests: even the oldest one is being taken apart and put together all the time.

science.text: A landscape under steady disturbance holds a steady mix of patches of different ages, while each patch keeps changing (Bormann and Likens, 1979).
An ecosystem can have more than one lasting state, so removing the cause of damage may not bring the old state back (Scheffer and others, from 1993).

other_view.who: Many conservationists, and Frederic Clements before them
other_view.view: Not all change is equal. An old forest holds beings that no young patch can, and some losses cannot be undone in a thousand years. To say 'everything always changes' can become an excuse for damage. There are better and worse states, and people should defend the better ones. Some go further and say that a forest that cannot return to what it was has not healed at all.

practice.title: Ending, beginning, staying
practice.say: Sit where you can see one plant: a tree from the window, or a pot. Look for one thing that is ending, such as a yellow leaf. Look for one thing that is beginning, such as a bud. Now look at the whole plant. Take three slow breaths. Each breath out is an ending, and each breath in is a beginning. The plant is still the plant, and you are still you.
practice.kid: Look at one plant. Find one thing that is ending. Find one thing that is beginning. Now take three slow breaths. Out is an ending. In is a beginning. You are still you.

playtest: The experiments, games and activities in this unit were reasoned through step by step, and the Patchwork Test was run on a computer. They have not yet been tried at home, so please treat the amounts and times as a starting point. The Patchwork Test (core) needs paper, a ruler, two dice and a notebook. A computer ran its rules 4,000 times. With 6 storms a round, old forest settled at 19 to 24 of the 36 patches from round 3 on. With 12 storms it settled at 10 to 16. Counting 36 squares after every round is the slow part, so work as a pair. The Soil Remembers depends on your soil. Soil from under weeds or from an old pot nearly always sprouts within ten days. Shop-bought potting mix may not. Roasting soil smells strongly. In Wetland on a Board, how much a towel holds depends on the towel, so the second and third tumblers may behave differently for you. In the Seed Ball Drop, a thick clay skin can stop every seed from sprouting. That is a result, not a failure. Climb to Old Forest takes 15 to 25 turns for each player. Facts checked by web search on 19 November 2026: the Yellowstone wolf releases, wolf, elk and beaver counts, and both sides of the willow argument. The Pichavaram dates and hectares. The Anamalai restoration and its 2019 results. The 2017 review of natural regrowth. Surtsey's first plant. The spider on Krakatau and the lupines of Mount St Helens. The Elwha dams. Pallikaranai's area. The dates of Cowles, Clements, Gleason and Davis. The cheetah arrivals at Kuno. The fern spores after the asteroid. The wording of Thirukkural 15, Dhammapada 277 and Heraclitus B12. All three video titles and channels. Not confirmed from a source in this session, and worth a second look: that elk avoid valleys out of fear is 'argued about', the smoke-sensing tobacco seeds, the Dutch lakes cleared by removing fish, the hornbill and macaque details on the game cards, and the exact way the ground at Pichavaram came to sink.
